title: Andy Reid Is Embracing a Simplified Approach After Chiefs' Complicated Loss to Broncos
full_text:
Despite controlling Sunday's Week 8 outing against the Denver Broncos for most of the afternoon, the Kansas City Chiefs couldn't get out of their own way. That trend only worsened into the early evening, culminating with a brutal loss on the road.
The 28-24 defeat brings Kansas City to 5-2 through seven games, also putting it behind its rivals in the AFC West standings for the first time all season. It's a loss that should hurt for a variety of reasons, especially with it being the result of numerous issues.
As he always does, though, head coach Andy Reid is taking the even-keeled route. Speaking to the media following Sunday's game, he emphasized the need to quickly turn the page and focus on what's ahead.
"Listen, things happen," Reid said. "There are a few more games left. We've got to make sure we rally from this, learn from it and then move on. That becomes important."
Reid singled out missed tackles and penalties as two things that Kansas City would benefit from cleaning up. At the same time, he alluded to his club still being right in the thick of it at the end, even after a compounding effect of mishaps set in.
"They made some plays there," Reid said. "I mentioned the tackling, we could've made some tackles. We were in position to do that; you've got to make those. Just like the other part of it is the penalties. You're playing a good football team, so when you do these things, you're not going to normally come out on the right end of it. We were in position to win the game, the penalty happened and we don't get the touchdown."
One can essentially take their pick of the litter when it comes to responsibility for this game's outcome. At a fundamental level, going on the road to Mile High and taking on a club that made the AFC title game earlier this calendar year is a challenge in and of itself. Finding a way to win when you commit 11 penalties for 105 yards and have a trio of three-and-outs further amplifies that.
Washing all of that down with a missed field goal, multiple poor fourth-down calls from the head coach and a defensive collapse at precisely the wrong time spells out doom. That's exactly what the Chiefs got, as they went from seemingly en route to a statement victory to getting punched in the mouth and having no suitable response.
The Broncos’ win probability fell to 10.2% early in the fourth quarter and was just 11.9% with 2:44 left in regulation in their comeback win over the Chiefs. Denver’s chances of winning the AFC West are now 64%. With a loss, they would have been 24%. Powered by @awscloud pic.twitter.com/yTc9UFmuQx
That's the kicker, though: Kansas City was remarkably close to still getting out of Dodge with a plus in the win column in the face of so many self-constructed roadblocks. It presents the team with a strange reality, as it showed several potential red flags while simultaneously lending credence to his unwavering belief that things will be corrected.
Reid actively served as a part of the problem in Week 8. His decision to punt on a short fourth down at his own 41-yard line was brought into question, as was his third-and-2 play call on the following drive that resulted in a sack on quarterback Patrick Mahomes (and a missed field goal by the struggling Harrison Butker ).
The offense, for yet another week, struggled to produce points under late-game pressure. The dam of the defense finally broke after Butker's miss. The special teams unit, obviously, was anything but special. Reid, tasked with putting his men in the best positions to succeed, didn't do that at the most important stages of the contest.
This doesn't have to become a lingering set of circumstances, but pressing the reset button immediately is paramount. It's one thing to say it and another to do it, although Reid's been on both sides of that coin.
Following a complicated loss, that's the simplicity of his message.
"I've got a good locker room," Reid said. "I know we work the right way here. We have to learn from it — that's what you do — and you move on. Work on the next one, which is a good Jets team coming in. We'll be ready to go."

title: 10 Instant Observations From Chiefs' Heartbreaking Week 8 Loss to Broncos
full_text:
Coming off their first loss of the season, the Kansas City Chiefs appeared to make a concerted effort to put forth a more inspiring performance. They managed to do so for most of Sunday against the Denver Broncos, although it wasn't in a winning effort.
Head coach Andy Reid's crew seemed to be in control for a good chunk of Week 8, only to fall short down the stretch and suffer a crushing defeat to a bitter rival.
With the 28-24 loss, the Chiefs fall to 5-2 on the year. Let's jump into 10 instant observations and takeaways from Week 8.
Blocking isn't the most head-turning element of the game, particularly for a skill-position player, but it should be discussed more. Especially for a team that operates in 12-personnel (one running back, two tight ends) with frequency, it's an important part of an offense. Travis Kelce, at age 37, being far and away the superior blocker between him and Noah Gray is an issue.
Gray's poor blocking chops showed up giaringly in the first half on two occasions — once in the run game and once in pass protection. Some of his shortcomings could be chalked up to a smaller and lighter frame , but his angles and leverage are oftentimes poor as well. This is a nitpick for someone who otherwise made an impact on Sunday, but it's long overdue to be mentioned.
Kansas City simultaneously flashed a much-improved offense over Week 7's production while also having a variety of rough moments that reminded everyone of why there's a long way to go. On one hand, quarterback Patrick Mahomes had a staggering 195 passing yards and two touchdowns. On the flip side, the Chiefs averaged only 3.5 yards per rush attempt and only kept the ball on the ground eight times.
Add in a 1-for-5 conversion clip on third down and there being three-and-outs on three separate occasions, and you get a more complete picture. This is a group that still needs to establish more consistency in play-calling decisions, execution, timing and more, but the first half of Week 8 was a step in the right direction. Not even a few dead drives in half No. 1 can take away from that.
Ending up with double-digit penalties for triple-digit yardage is inexcusable. Sure, one ticky-tacky holding call on right guard Trey Smith made up part of that total, but that doesn't explain the rest of the bunch from Sunday.
Some infractions were more procedural in nature, such as a false start on Kelce, an illegal formation charged to left tackle Kahlil Benson and an ineligible man downfield flag on right tackle Jaylon Moore. Others, though, were worse and simply cannot be repeated. Linebacker Jack Cochrane and safety Alohi Gilman each had unnecessary roughness penalties in Week 8, making life harder than necessary for the defense.
Some special teams issues and a rough outing for cornerback Kristian Fulton didn't help matters one bit. Moore's false start on a fourth-and-goal at the end of the game was the not-so-sweet icing on the cake.
Last week, I wrote a bit about defensive end Ashton Gillotte as someone whose stock is on the rise . Truthfully, it's easy to forget that he sustained a plantar fascia injury during training camp and started the 2026-27 campaign at a slow pace. He's ramped that up in a big way in recent weeks, however, and this game was no different.
Gillotte had a good run stop on Denver's opening drive, made a quality read on its second possession and also chipped in on a double-effort run stop in the second quarter that wasn't credited in the box score. The sophomore man continues to prove that he's a starting-caliber player, which is great for the Kansas City defensive line.
One thing that All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones made a name for himself for early in his career was tipping passes at the line of scrimmage. When defensive end George Karlaftis entered the league in 2022, his water polo background was brought up on broadcasts seemingly every week. That history continues to pay off years later, evidenced by two pass breakups in the second frame on Sunday.
Rookie pass rusher R Mason Thomas also had a batted pass on the Broncos' third drive. Defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga notched one in the third quarter to help cap off his solid day at the office. This is clearly something defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo and defensive line coach Joe Cullen emphasize, which pays off.
For weeks, plenty of folks who follow the Chiefs (this writer included) have wondered when rookie running back Emmett Johnson 's breakout would occur. It was only a matter of time before he found a way to make an impact, and he had a multitude of signature moments over the course of Sunday afternoon and evening to make his presence known in a huge way.
Starting with the supporting elements of his game, the Nebraska product had an amazing 15-yard run that looked reminiscent of many from starter Kenneth Walker III. On special teams, he had a 44-yard kickoff return late in the fourth quarter that helped put the offense in a great starting position. It was Johnson's output in the receiving game, though, that made a huge difference.
The first-year man was excellent out of the backfield, taking a beautiful pass from Mahomes to the house for 73 yards and also adding a 38-yarder near halftime. In the fourth frame, he recorded a third-and-2 reception to move the chains as well. If there was ever a week for Johnson to establish himself as a viable option down the stretch, it was this one.
THE ROOKIE EMMETT JOHNSON WITH A 73-YARD TD KCvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/sGCPC0rJYU
Rookie wideout Cyrus Allen got some more run in this one and even had a nice eight-yard reception on an out route in the third quarter. A clutch third-and-12 snag also provided a glimpse of the possible chain-moving, reliable threat he can become if he realizes his potential.
With that said, the Cincinnati alum seemed to slow up early on a deep pass from Mahomes. Perhaps Allen just didn't think the ball was coming his way and was too late to realize it was, but it was a rough look either way. A play like that could've given him a totally different stat line and earned him some good graces with Mahomes and the coaching staff, so it's undoubtedly a missed opportunity.
When the Chiefs brought in kicker Justin Tucker on the practice squad this week, it sent a clear message that starter Harrison Butker was on thin ice with the organization. Reid shot down high-level concerns regarding the longtime franchise favorite following Week 7's loss, but it might be time to push the conversation forward even more.
Sure, some rain made Butker's 54-yard field goal in the fourth quarter more difficult, but he's paid handsomely to make these kicks under pressure. That miss swung momentum to Denver's favor and things quickly devolved from there, so part of this loss falls squarely on the veteran placekicker's shoulders. His seat has to be warming up even more.
There's plenty of blame to go around in this one. The aforementioned penalties were a killer at various points in the contest, and Reid did himself and his team very few favors with how he managed the fourth quarter.
disaster 4th quarter from the Chiefs they didn't go for this, but asked Harrison Butker to hit a 54 yard FG on the next series https://t.co/w27sbvGdBR
You can lump in the defense's poor — and rapidly poor — response to the Butker miss into the pile, too. For a team that's led by vets both on the paying surface and on the sideline, this one stings. It's easily one of the more prominent and obvious collapses of the Reid-Mahomes era.
Don't get it twisted: Kansas City isn't doomed in the division race by any stretch of the imagination. That said, failing to maintain the head-to-head tiebreaker over a hot Broncos team is suboptimal. Rising to 4-0 in the AFC West and creating more padding to kick off the month of November would've been massive for a team that's now floundering just a bit.

title: Complete Chiefs Inactives for Week 8 vs. Broncos: Mansoor Delane and Others Out on Sunday
full_text:
For the fourth time in seven games, the Kansas City Chiefs are clashing with an AFC West rival on the gridiron. Sunday features a Week 8 matchup with the Denver Broncos , marking the second and final instance of the two sides seeing one another in the regular season.
Just like they did in Week 1's 31-10 drubbing of Denver in Week 1, injuries play a role in how this one unfolds. Kansas City is down a top starter on the defensive side of the ball, with Denver also missing a key secondary piece in addition to placing a promising young player on injured reserve.
With that in mind, here's who's inactive for Kansas City and Denver in Sunday's matchup.
Our inactives for today's Week 8 matchup against the Denver Broncos ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/YGrIHpkCKr
Earlier in the week , Kansas City deemed cornerbacks L'Jarius Sneed and Mansoor Delane questionable while also tagging edge rusher R Mason Thomas with the same designation. On Saturday, however, the team announced that Sneed was going on the injured reserve list with a knee issue and Delane was downgraded to out.
Thomas, who traveled separately after attending to a personal matter, is in Denver and will be active for Sunday's game.
Although he doesn't appear on the inactives list, defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott was ruled out after being a limited participant in practice this week. The sophomore lineman was designated to return from the physically unable to perform list on Wednesday, marking a huge step in his ongoing recovery from a torn ACL.
The good news is receiver Rashee Rice is back in the lineup after not having played since Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders. The star wideout, who's nursed a hamstring injury , has 13 receptions for 190 yards and a touchdown in four games this year.
👀 our inactives for #KCvsDEN . 📰 » https://t.co/NPfgwIa5vk pic.twitter.com/4c24nidQc3
The Broncos' injury situation is less than ideal, to say the least. Rolling into the weekend, four players were questionable, including wide receiver Jaylen Waddle (chest), tackle Garett Bolles (hip) and defensive end Zach Allen (hamstring). All three, on top of safety Brandon Jones, were limited participants in practice to end the week.
Safety Talanoa Hufanga (ankle) didn't practice all week and was ruled out for Sunday. Second-year running back RJ Harvey, who sustained a knee injury in practice this week, is out and has since been moved to IR. He'll miss the next three Broncos games after Week 8.

title: Chiefs vs. Broncos: NFL Week 8 Preview, Score Predictions
full_text:
To kick off the 2026-27 campaign, the Kansas City Chiefs secured a statement victory over the Denver Broncos in blowout fashion. Replicating that performance is going to be much easier said than done in the rematch, however, especially with Andy Reid's team hitting the road.
Denver seems to be finding its stride just a little bit, although a win over the Arizona Cardinals won't convince anyone that the reigning division champions are all the way back.
The winner of Sunday's tilt could generate some serious momentum in the AFC West race as the season approaches its midpoint. What gives in the afternoon window of play?
The Kansas City Chiefs On SI crew makes its predictions for Week 8 of the regular season.
Joshua Brisco: For the second week in a row, I'm expecting a low-scoring game. This time, however, I think the Chiefs will find the end zone. Kansas City just needs enough from Rashee Rice and his fellow pass catchers to allow Kenneth Walker to have opportunities similar to the ones he took advantage of in Week 1. The final inactives list will be massive for both teams, but I expect the Chiefs to escape Denver with a narrow win.
Jordan Foote: Getting wideout Rashee Rice back in the fold for this one is huge. Given that Xavier Worthy's come back down to earth, Travis Kelce is banged up and Kenneth Walker III has finally looked human, having a formidable weapon on offense is paramount. On the other side of the ball, missing cornerback Mansoor Delane will hurt, but being minus L'Jarius Sneed might just be an addition-by-subtraction scenario.
Expect a one-score game that is far from the prettiest, albeit with Kansas City still doing enough to complete the sweep of Denver and maintain first place in the AFC West.
Joshua Schulman: The Chiefs are reeling after an ugly loss to Seattle in prime time last week. It’s difficult to imagine the offense looking any more inept than it did a week ago when it mustered just one field goal all night. The Broncos’ defense isn’t quite as dominant as Seattle’s but still is a formidable unit. With that said, we saw who the better team was when these two sides met in Week 1.
Denver has been winning in spite of Bo Nix’s play, not because of it, and the KC coaching staff has to have stressed the importance of a game in which it could lose the first-place lead in the AFC West.
Tyler Brown: This feels like a tighter game than Week 1, but the Chiefs' strengths match up well against those of the Broncos. Denver will be desperate with the divisional stakes swinging so heavily. With Jonathan Cooper lined up opposite Nik Bonitto, the Broncos have a better edge-rush pairing than they did in September, which puts the Chiefs’ tackle situation under real stress if it ends up in too many obvious dropback situations.
The Broncos may perform better this go-around, but the matchup tilts toward the Chiefs. Denver’s rushing defense ranks 28th and leads the league in missed tackles, which is exactly the situation Kenneth Walker thrives in.
Getting Rashee Rice back is a bigger deal than it may sound, because it gives Patrick Mahomes another reliable weapon and it lets Xavier Worthy and the rest of the group settle into their roles.
On the other side, Denver is 30th in total offense and 25th in scoring, and Nix has struggled when pressured, especially against the blitz. If Steve Spagnuolo gets creative and some pass rushers outside of George Karlaftis step up, that is another major Chiefs advantage.

title: Chiefs' Cornerback Depth Takes Considerable Hit With Latest Injury News
full_text:
A pleasant surprise of the Kansas City Chiefs' season thus far has been their cornerback room. For the most part, players like Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams are providing surplus value and helping shape what could turn out to be a premier duo for years to come.
One weakness of the unit, however, is the slot position. Veteran L'Jarius Sneed, who signed back with his first NFL franchise earlier this year, has struggled in his second stint with the team. Unfortunately, he won't have an opportunity to improve that level of play in the next handful of weeks.
Per a post on X from the Chiefs on Saturday, Sneed is going on the injured reserve list. As a result, he'll miss at least Sunday's contest versus the Denver Broncos and upcoming games against the New York Jets, Atlanta Falcons and Arizona Cardinals.
We have signed Practice Squad player CB Melvin Smith to an active roster contract. We have activated Practice Squad player DE Tyreke Smith via Standard Elevation. We have placed CB L’Jarius Sneed on Reserve/Injured. pic.twitter.com/oczbgGKFOf
Taking Sneed's place on the active 53-man roster is practice squad cornerback Melvin Smith. In the same sweep of announcements, Kansas City revealed that defensive end Tyreke Smith was activated from the practice squad via standard elevation.
Sneed, who turns 30 in January, has 32 tackles and three pass breakups across 258 defensive snaps in the Chiefs' six games this year. According to NFL Pro , offenses have targeted Sneed on 29.2% of his coverage snaps, the highest rate for anyone with 100-plus reps since at least 2018. Pro Football Focus is harsh on his coverage, too, citing him with 36 receptions and a 110.0 passer rating given up.
The news doesn't stop there for the Chiefs, as their top 2026 NFL Draft pick will also sit out this weekend's clash in Denver.
In a separate post , Kansas City shared that rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane was downgraded to out for Week 8 due to a shoulder injury. It's something that's been an off-and-on issue for months, with head coach Andy Reid saying Friday the team would " see how he does " before making a final decision on his Sunday availability.
Delane, the No. 6 overall pick in April's draft, recorded an interception on the very first drive of his NFL career in Week 1's blowout win over these same Broncos. The LSU product has played 287 defensive snaps for coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, good for 83% of those available, in his five games.
Delane's had a very strong debut season overall but did get his proverbial " welcome to the league " moment(s) against the Seattle Seahawks and reigning Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba in Week 7.
When asked about the opportunity to line up against elite wideouts, Delane said he embraces the challenge to hone his craft.
"I think some people may get discouraged from passes caught on them," Delane said. "But I told coach Spags, ‘Man, put me in those tough situations.’ I'm not asking for a cloud. I'm not asking for Cover 2. Go back out there and play man, and that's what we did. A lot of teams [are] kind of scared to do that, but I feel like we didn't shy away from it. We learned from it, but at the same time, there are going to be times in my career that I'm going to better handle that stick, and I'm definitely going to learn from that.”
It's unclear whether Delane's injury will hold him out of Week 9's meeting with the Jets; his practice participation next week should give a stronger signal either way.
To cap off this injury roundup, second-round defensive end R Mason Thomas (personal) will travel separately and join the team in the Mile High City.

title: Ranking the Chiefs Players Most Likely to Be Traded Before the Deadline
full_text:
While all 32 NFL teams are primarily banking on their internal candidates to either sustain momentum or help turn things around, there's still time to acquire some assistance from the outside. For clubs like the Kansas City Chiefs, a trade might be what makes or breaks the season.
As the calendar flips from October to November, the NFL trade deadline (November 10, 3:00 p.m. CT) is rapidly approaching. With needs at wide receiver and potentially elsewhere, could general manager Brett Veach make any moves to improve the roster?
If not, what about recouping some NFL Draft capital for the future and shedding a bit of weight in the process? Chiefs On SI has singled out five Kansas City players who might be appealing to other organizations for various reasons ahead of the cutoff.
When the Chiefs first signed cornerback Kristian Fulton to a two-year deal in the 2025 offseason, this couldn't have been the path they envisioned. The former Los Angeles Chargers standout was hurt coming into the year and spent most of the season buried on the bench, only to show flashes at the end of the campaign and leave just as many questions as answers entering the spring and summer.
Seven weeks into the 2026-27 regular season, has Fulton managed to clear anything up? It's complicated. He's been available for 135 defensive snaps — 40% of those possible — and has surrendered just four completions on eight targets for 18 yards ( Pro Football Reference ). He's served primarily as depth, although L'Jarius Sneed's struggles and rookie Mansoor Delane's fluctuating health might make Fulton someone to keep around.
Still, per Spotrac , Fulton only has $5.42 million remaining on his deal and could be an intriguing pickup for any corner-needy club. He easily makes the most sense as a trade chip, in this writer's view.
Update: Sneed has since been placed on the injured reserve list , further emphasizing the potential need for Fulton.
Considering that quarterback Justin Fields has played only one regular-season snap as a Chief, any team acquiring him would be doing so strictly out of circumstance or approval of his past performance. The last time we saw the former first-round pick for an extended stretch was this preseason, when he went 13-for-16 passing for 105 yards. Prior to that, it was a nine-game starting stint with the New York Jets that saw him own an 89.5 passer rating.
Still, Fields remains a mobile dual-threat signal-caller with experience in a multitude of offenses. If there's a franchise out there with an injured starter or a pressing need for a backup, making a swap like this is sensible. He's a free agent in the spring, so this wouldn't net anything more than a very late draft pick.
It's hard to see Fields being dealt twice in one calendar year, but weirder things have happened.
For one reason or another, the Chiefs' original fourth-round selection of tight end Jared Wiley in 2024 hasn't panned out. The former TCU product battled injury earlier in his Kansas City tenure, and he's been primarily a warm body in the position room in 2026. Entering Week 8's showdown with the Denver Broncos, Wiley's appeared in one game, playing seven snaps on special teams and two on offense.
Is there a team out there that thinks it can unlock something with Wiley? He turns 26 two days after the publication of this story and has one year remaining on his deal after 2026. Perhaps an offensive coaching staff is optimistic it can harness whatever's left of his athletic profile and make him a decidely rosterable player.
Jared Wiley is a TE prospect in the 2024 draft class. He scored an unofficial  9.52 #RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 55 out of 1116 TE from 1987 to 2024. Splits projected https://t.co/AUYy1C4co1 pic.twitter.com/GYtwZ0nzRn
I personally don't believe Wiley has any trade value, but again, it's hard to completely rule out.
The case of safety Jaden Hicks, another 2024 fourth-rounder, is curious. As a rookie, he looked like a budding star at the position, yet he's been anything but that ever since. Last year was a rough one for him, although he went on to produce some highlights this preseason and got a vote of confidence from defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo in the process.
Hicks' workload is at a career-high 69% mark by snap share, although it's down to 41.6% over his last three games. Pro Football Focus credits him with nine "stops" in six contests, paired with a healthy 77.5 tackling grade, although his coverage chops are still questionable at best.
Given that Chamarri Conner is slated to become a free agent in March, it may not be too wise an idea for Kansas City to give up on Hicks right now. Should an opposing executive come with a surprising offer, however, Veach would have to at least consider it.
This one seems like the most difficult needle to thread in terms of likelihood. Not only can defensive back Chris Roland-Wallace do a bit of everything in the secondary, but he's a Spagnuolo favorite and also plays for Dave Toub's special teams unit. Add in that he's entering restricted free agency in the spring, and it makes more sense for the Chiefs to retain those rights and leave it up to the market than move him in 2026.
For all the play-related reasons, though, Roland-Wallace might appeal to another front office. This season, in particular, he's been a heat-seeking missile on screen passes and is always a threat to crash downhill with reckless abandon. He's lined up 48 times in the box, 40 in the slot and 12 along the edge of the defensive line. Last year, he had 60 reps as a traditional free safety as well.
Finding a cost-effective jack of all trades is infinitely easier said than done.

title: The Chiefs’ Biggest Matchup on Each Side of the Ball Against the Broncos
full_text:
The Chiefs' Week 8 trip to Denver is as big a mid-season game as Kansas City has played in recent memory.
According to The Athletic’s 2026 NFL Simulator , the Chiefs’ odds of winning the AFC West skyrocket to 84 percent with a win over the Broncos. With a loss, those odds drop to 48 percent, and the race likely stays neck and neck until the end of the season.
The Broncos will be a desperate opponent, which is always a scary situation for a team like Kansas City. In the same vein, head coach Andy Reid and defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo understand the magnitude of the game, so they likely will not hold back either.
Here are the two biggest matchups the Chiefs could exploit to take complete control of the AFC West.
The Chiefs found out last week what happens when an opponent shuts down its rushing attack. It may have been a matchup issue, and no defense in the league may be better suited to shut down Kenneth Walker than the Seattle Seahawks . Slowing him down is much easier said than done.
With the run game not working, Reid handed it to Kenneth Walker just 14 times, even though it was a tight ballgame for most of the contest. They got away from many of the under-center formations that had been working.
Walker finished with 36 yards, a season low by far. That led Patrick Mahomes to attempt 33 passes in a predictable game plan that Seattle had no trouble figuring out, and it visibly frustrated Mahomes and the Kansas City offense.
Denver defensive coordinator Vance Joseph will surely not deploy the same strategy he did in Week 1, when the Chiefs scored 31 points and Walker ran for 173 yards. That said, the Broncos are the league's 28th-ranked rushing defense. Walker forced 14 missed tackles in that Week 1 game, and the tackling woes have continued for Joseph’s defense.
Denver leads the league in missed tackles with 60 through seven games. There will be adjustments, but this may simply be a great matchup for the Kansas City offense. Walker is still second in the NFL in rushing yards, and he should pick up right where he left off before Week 7.
This matchup is a similar theme. The Chiefs got after the quarterback against Denver in Week 1, but they couldn’t do it at all against the Seahawks.
While Kansas City’s defense still ranks among the league’s best in pressure rate, they are second-to-last in total sacks with eight. Oddly enough, they have two games with four sacks and four games where they were completely blanked. Luckily for the Chiefs, one of those four-sack games came against the Broncos and Bo Nix.
Nix has been sacked only four times in the six games since, but he has performed poorly when pressured, which clearly plays into what Kansas City’s pass rush has actually been able to accomplish.
According to PFF, when kept clean, Nix has six touchdowns and one interception. When pressured, he has one touchdown and two interceptions. When pressured, he has six more turnover-worthy plays, a quarterback rating 53.2 points worse, and gets the ball out nearly a full second slower.
Many of those poor numbers have come against the blitz. Nix has been blitzed on 90 dropbacks this season, averaging just 4.1 yards per attempt with a 46 percent completion rate, and he has been sacked three times in those instances.
With so much riding on this game, Spagnuolo could unleash some of his patented exotic blitzes. The biggest question marks are how creative he is with his calls and whether Chris Jones can finally get going, or whether it will once again be the George Karlaftis show, with a splash of pressure from R Mason Thomas.
If Kansas City can get back to pressuring Nix, the offense may not need its best day to win. Keeping Denver’s offense stuck where it has been all season, 30th in total offense and 25th in scoring, is the number one key to this game.

title: Mike McDaniel, Justin Herbert and Chargers Winners and Losers Before NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers had another opportunity to get back on track Sunday, but things went from promising to disappointing. Despite taking an early lead against the Los Angeles Rams, the Chargers couldn’t find the end zone. In the NFL, touchdowns win you games, not field goals.
There were a few individual performances worth recognizing, but the bigger concern is becoming impossible to ignore.
The Chargers have now gone two consecutive games without scoring a touchdown, and the offense looks like it is running out of answers.
It’s been nine quarters since the Chargers offense has scored a TD. No way you can win games like that.
If there was one offensive player who gave the Chargers something to be excited about, it was McConkey. The third-year receiver finished with four receptions for 86 yards, including an impressive 54-yard catch that gave a major opportunity to put points on the board before halftime.
When healthy, this guy can be a highly reliable target.
McConkey continues to show why he should be one of the focal points of this offense. His ability to create separation and make plays downfield is something the team desperately needs right now. When you’re one of the few players consistently creating opportunities, you deserve to be recognized.
Dicker continues to be one of the most dependable players on this roster.
The Chargers kicker converted all three of his field goal attempts, accounting for every point Los Angeles scored against the Rams.
It’s obviously not an ideal situation when your kicker is responsible for your entire scoring output, but Dicker did exactly what was asked of him. He made his opportunities count while the offense struggled to get anything going. There isn’t much more you can ask from him.
Herbert needs to be better. There is no way around that conversation after Sunday’s performance. The Chargers quarterback threw for 257 yards but also surrendered two interceptions. Both of which came at difficult moments for an offense already struggling to find consistency.
The offensive problems extend well beyond Herbert, but he is still the franchise quarterback. Those types of players have to be the bright spot of the team during these situations. Herbert has the talent to change the direction of this offense, but the team needs to start seeing that translate into results.
The Chargers brought McDaniel in to help give this offense a new identity, but the results have been nowhere near good enough. Another game without a touchdown is going to raise serious questions about what exactly this offensive system is trying to accomplish.
There needs to be more creativity, better adjustments, and a much clearer plan for getting the football into the hands of the team’s best playmakers. Having Herbert under center should give this offense a significant advantage, yet they continue to look completely out of rhythm. McDaniel has to find a solution before this season gets any further out of hand.
The offensive line has become one of the biggest reasons this offense cannot establish any consistency.
The Chargers cannot expect Herbert to constantly manufacture plays when the protection and blocking aren’t giving him much help. The lack of production on the ground is becoming a weekly problem, and it is putting additional pressure on everyone else. This unit needs to start winning its battles up front.
Hampton had another frustrating afternoon, finishing with just 20 rushing yards on nine carries. The rookie has shown flashes of what he can become, but performances like this aren’t going to help an offense desperately searching for consistency.
The scheme this year has never been in his favor, so that cannot help at all. There are many factors for his lack of production.
The offensive line certainly deserves some of the blame, but Hampton also needs to find ways to make something happen when the running lanes aren’t perfect.
The Chargers are 0-7, and welcome in a Houston team next Sunday that's 2-5, back against the wall and coming off a bye. They've been steadfast with other teams on not being a seller. But ...
Brennan is sports writer focused on delivering sharp analysis, real-time reactions, and engaging storytelling focused on NFL analysis.  He is passionate about football and breaking down what matters to bring fans closer to the action.  Brennan comes from a family of Chargers fans.

title: Justin Herbert Benched? Chargers Are So Bad The Topic's Starting to Emerge
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have fallen to 0-7 after a poor performance against their cross-town rival, the Los Angeles Rams. With both teams falling short of their preseason expectations, it seemed that both teams were hungry for some sort of victory, with the Chargers looking for their first.
Obviously, the Chargers did not win the game, continuing the trend of embarrassing performances, even with the team coming off their bye week. A major cog in this embarrassment, seen throughout the entire season, has been what was seemingly the team's best player: QB Justin Herbert .
Herbert has been the team's starting QB since his rookie season in 2020. During this time, he has won Offensive Rookie of the Year, earned multiple Pro Bowl selections and has received MVP votes. It is obvious that the 2020 sixth overall selection has the talent and ability to be an NFL all-time great.
The issue is that the 2026 season has been a decline that we have never seen before. If you told the fanbase that the offense would be terrible prior to the season, the majority of fans would assume it would be everyone but Herbert's fault. I would be in the same boat as those fans.
But unfortunately, the 2026 season has been largely Herbert's fault. It is important to include the context of injuries and horrid coaching around him, but it has gotten to the point where Herbert is completely unable to overcome those issues as he has before.
This season has Herbert leading the league in interceptions, while being among the league low in passing yards and touchdowns for starters around the league. This week, against the Rams, Herbert threw for 257 yards, a season high. Unfortunately, this came with zero touchdowns and two interceptions, with both of those interceptions being indefensible. Thrown straight to a defender.
With this context and poor performance in Week 8, reporter Eric Williams asked a brutal question regarding the idea of benching Herbert for Jim Harbaugh after the game, and Harbaugh responded with "No." More context is seen below in Williams' tweet about the interaction.
I asked Jim Harbaugh if he considered benching Justin Herbert and he said “No.” On continuing to let Mike McDaniel calling plays, Harbaugh said it’s a team effort, that most players in the locker room have never been in this position before and they will keep working. pic.twitter.com/9czq89eJYl
Okay, so Harbaugh says no to benching Herbert. That is the correct thing to do. The issue is that Herbert is now being placed in benching conversations, conversations that are now known to his head coach. This is not great territory to be in for anyone, let alone a guy who was once a 5,000-yard passer and is currently the face of the Chargers franchise.

title: Chargers Players Rising, Falling After Week 8 Loss, Impact on NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are now 0-7, still being the only team without a win in the 2026 NFL season. With another disappointing loss added to their season, who were some players who either helped cause the loss or tried their hardest for the team to finally get a win?
While injuries are always a bad thing, one of the few positives that come from players missing time is that the players replacing them get a chance to show what they've got. Usually, these players are down the depth chart and down there for a reason, but rarely you will find a guy like Isas Waxter .
Waxter is making his first NFL start as the team's third corner, with the team missing Donte Jackson, Deane Leonard, Rodney Shelley and Derwin James all missing the game. In his first NFL start, Waxter showed major heart, showing reliable yet aggressive tackling ability while not being obviously burnt in coverage.
Waxter's statline against the Rams: Six tackles, two of which were for loss.
Jake Slaughter was the team's second-round selection in the 2026 NFL Draft, and one of the team's more criticized selections. It was less because of Slaughter's ability as a player and more because of the plan for him. He was expected to make the transition from center to guard and compete for a spot in camp.
Drafting a player to purposefully move him away from where he has been at his best at the collegiate level is questionable at best. Even with this, Slaughter found his way on the field, moving back to center after the Tyler Biadasz injury. Since he has taken over, there have been a plethora of rookie growing pains , with this game against the Rams being one of his worst.
Jake Slaughter got beat instantly on that 3rd & 1. He falls due to his whiff and doesn't get back up. He stays on the ground and sulks instead. Sounds about right for this offense.
Whether it was playing poorly in the run game, missing defenders, or genuinely playing 'soft,' Slaughter was outmatched this week. The Chargers can only hope for Slaughter to improve as the season continues, as this level of play is unacceptable.
Ladd McConkey finally had a full game back after the slew of injuries he suffered early in the season. In Week 8, he was able to have a strong game against the Los Angeles Rams and their secondary that boasts Trent McDuffie and Quentin Lake.
McConkey was the lone bright spot of the offense, earning four catches for a team-high 86 yards. If healthy, McConkey is expected to continue helping this offense try to be better than the league-worst.
Elijah Molden has been a very confounding player for the Chargers, having immense ups and downs with the team, with many of the downs being injury-related. Once signed to a new contract extension, Molden has been very hit-or-miss while on the field.
Today against the Rams, Molden had multiple crucial missed tackles, poor run fits and no splash plays in coverage. It was a rough day for the veteran safety, not performing well with his running mate Derwin James Jr. being out.

title: Mike McDaniel’s ‘All-Hands’ Meeting Might Be Saddest Chargers Story Yet
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are in a bad, bad way.
Jim Harbaugh’s Chargers are 0-6 coming out of a bye with little in the way of changed plans except for staying the course. Things are so samey around the Chargers that even other teams are confused about how they’re approaching the NFL trade deadline.
Maybe the only silver lining for the Chargers right now is the fact they clutch the No. 1 pick in next year’s draft, at least for now. There’s plenty of cap space, too, though whether they use it to get aggressive during a possible rebuild next offseason will have fans justifiably skeptical.
Now is the time of a season like this where the stories start coming out about how the Chargers got innovative to turn the season around.
The 2026 version of this story for the Chargers, though, is pretty alarming.
The Chargers didn't get creative during the bye week. They kept things the same, doubling down on pretty much everything, including offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel.
And McDaniel? He held an “all-hands” meeting with his offense.
The topic? Reviewing training camp practice footage .
According to The Athletic’s Noah Furtado , the big Monday meeting was a notable one.
“For over an hour, the Los Angeles Chargers studied more than a dozen snaps from their joint practice with the San Francisco 49ers, a team not on their schedule for another couple of months,” Furtado wrote.
So, in near-November at 0-6, the Chargers grouped up and watched August film from a joint-practice where sacks didn’t count. They beat up on the 49ers that day, yes, but they went on to lose six straight real games while those 49ers won six straight.
Whatever messaging McDaniel was trying to achieve gets a little lost in the context. Justin Herbert is still tied for the most interceptions (eight) and turnovers (10) in the NFL despite the bye, among many other horrific stats.
McDaniel and Herbert, per Furtado, linked up for a pair of two-hour film review sessions during the bye, so there’s that.
We’ve mentioned before that firing McDaniel mid-season might not actually accomplish much at this point. But the fact the big all-hands meeting meant to inspire change was a film review of a summer practice session really speaks to just how far off the rails this Chargers season has gone.

title: The End of the Road: Latest Roster Moves Signal Multiple Chargers Done for the Year
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are set to take on the Los Angeles Rams in week eight. The Chargers, coming off a bye in week seven, have dealt with significant injuries in the first half of the season and had over half of the original 53-man roster on the injury report or injured reserve by week six.
Los Angeles will see some limited reinforcements return to the field against the Rams but the injuries have continued to mount and several have suffered setbacks. The most notable setbacks have been to team leader and All-Pro defensive back Derwin James Jr. and to rookie wide receiver Brenan Thompson.
full game status for week 8 at LAR pic.twitter.com/kRgRS940zR
James was placed on injured reserve on the eve of the game against the Rams and Thompson, out since week two, tried to return in week five only to suffer a setback, was surprisingly active for week six but logged zero snaps and now has suffered another setback in rehab with a hamstring injury being added on to his quad injury.
The Chargers decision to move Derwin James to injured reserve is peculiar in timing considering he has been out since Week 3. The NFL rules stipulate that teams are allowed eight activations from the injured list per season and two additional activations for the postseason. The Chargers do not appear to be poised to make the postseason therefore they have a maximum of eight activations off of injured reserve and have already used three of them.
Los Angeles has already activated offensive lineman Branson Taylor and fullback/tight end Scott Matlock, both of whom were placed on injured reserve to start the season. In addition to Taylor and Matlock, the Chargers activated wide receiver Keandre Lambert-Smith.
James being added to injured reserve now leaves the Chargers with eight players from their original 53-man roster on injured reserve with only five activations remaining. Of those eight players six were considered starters. Tyler Biadasz is clearly done for the season but of the other players, who has played their last snaps for the 2026 Chargers? •	Defensive back Derwin James Jr. •	Fullback Alec Ingold •	Offensive lineman Trey Pipkins III •	Linebacker Denzel Perryman •	Quarterback Trey Lance •	Offensive lineman Trevor Penning •	Tight end David Njoku •	Tackle Rashawn Slater
There are so many unanswered questions with this group of players. If the season is lost, is it worth it to rush Rashawn Slater, who is already coming off major injury, back onto the field? Derwin James is a cornerstone player. Alec Ingold was intended to be the glue of the blocking department but did not look good when healthy. Pipkins and Penning have essentially been replaced by rookies.
The Chargers are only entering Week 8, there is no telling how many more players will end up on injured reserve. Who Los Angeles brings back to the active roster with their five remaining activations will be a major chess move for the remainder of the season and likely an indication of intentions for the upcoming offseason.
Not only could several of these players have played their last snaps for the 2026 Chargers, several of them are on expiring deals or deals with a contract out in the offseason. There is a high likelihood that several of these players on injured reserve have played their last snaps in Los Angeles.

title: Chargers Confidence Meter: A Win Against the Rams Could Mean A Lot For Their Future
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have an opportunity to finally secure a win and silence a small portion of doubt. A matchup against the Los Angeles Rams could have a much bigger impact on how the rest of their season unfolds.
Especially when it comes to the team’s confidence , playoff outlook, and even their future draft position.
For the Chargers, this is the type of game that can help determine what kind of team they really are. Facing another competitive team gives them an opportunity to prove they can put together a complete performance when it matters.
One of the biggest things the Chargers need to focus on is establishing consistency on both sides of the football. Offensively, they need to give Herbert opportunities to make plays without putting the entire responsibility on his shoulders. Establishing the run game, protecting the quarterback, and finding ways to create explosive plays will be important against a Rams defense that can make things difficult.
Defensively, the Chargers cannot afford to let the Rams dictate the pace of the game. Getting pressure on the quarterback, limiting explosive plays, and forcing difficult third-down situations could make a significant difference. Games like this are often decided by which team makes fewer mistakes. The Bolts are dealing with secondary issues, so that certainly does not help. Defensive Coordinator Chris O’Leary has a great scheme and should be able to adjust to the situation regardless.
However there is one main caveat.
If the Chargers continue winning games, their position in the upcoming draft could change significantly. While a better draft position can give a rebuilding team access to higher selections. They are in a position where competing and building momentum should be the priority. Winning games can also help the organization evaluate its current roster and identify which positions actually need attention when draft season arrives.
There is always a balance between winning now and building for the future. The Chargers want to be a team competing for championships, and getting meaningful wins against quality opponents is part of that process. A victory over the Rams would not automatically solve every issue surrounding the team, but it could provide another reason to believe in what this roster is capable of accomplishing.
This is bigger than just another game on the schedule.
The Chargers have an opportunity to make a statement, build confidence, and give themselves something to carry into the second half of the season. Now they have to go out and prove it.

title: NFL Trade Rumors Say Chargers’ Weird Behavior Confuses Other Teams, Too
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers entered this season looking a little lost and confused and have wound up confusing their own fanbase with their approach to the NFL trade deadline , too.
Now…the Chargers are confusing other teams at the deadline, too.
All of the rumors and buzz and speculation so far around the NFL trade deadline have made it clear that the Chargers, in fact, are not looking to sell off any pieces despite sitting at 0-6 and first in the NFL draft order.
That, while not choosing to make any changes over a bye week with names like offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel.
Now, the rumor mill is even reporting about the confusion other teams have about the confusing Chargers.
The Chargers aren’t selling.
That much has been obvious. But here’s a fun follow-up from The Athletic’s Jonathan Jones : “The Chargers have confounded teams by not engaging in trade talks. The Bolts are 0-6 but are telling teams Khalil Mack isn’t available. It’s hard to envision that remaining the case over the next 10 days.”
Things are so weird around the Chargers that they’re confounding other teams.
Here’s where there is an actual concern. It’s one thing to publicly posture like a team won’t sell. No need for the negative PR or to hint to the locker room that this is a lost cause and the franchise is waving a white flag. Plenty of teams act like this in public but still talk the trade talk behind the scenes and off the record.
The fact the Chargers have other teams shocked with how they’re moving behind the scenes feels problematic, though. If they’re shutting down any and all trade talk, even off the record, it concerningly matches their lack of change in the face of problems at 0-6.
The Chargers can’t afford to sit still and do nothing . They have one of, if not the worst, rosters in football. They’re sitting on cap space they won’t spend and also hoarding trade assets like Khalil Mack who, frankly, deserves to go to a better organization.
Selling off at 0-6 clears the books, adds future assets, clears more playing time for younger players and boosts the odds of landing the No. 1 pick. Remaining this adamant about not selling, to the point other teams are a little surprised about how they’re moving, is perhaps the most damning thing about the Chargers in 2026.

title: Fantasy Football Start or Sit: Don't Give Up On Omarion Hampton Just Yet
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have an important matchup ahead of them in Week 8 as they prepare to take on the Los Angeles Rams.
For fantasy football managers, there are a handful of Chargers players worth keeping an eye on.
However, some options are considerably more appealing than others . Here’s a look at five Chargers players and whether they deserve a spot in your starting lineup this week.
Omarion Hampton remains one of the more interesting fantasy options on this Chargers offense. Through six games, Hampton has recorded 289 rushing yards and three touchdowns on 80 carries.
The biggest concern has been his efficiency, averaging just 3.6 yards per carry. Still, his workload gives him opportunities to produce, especially if the Chargers can establish their running game early.
Hampton isn’t necessarily somebody I would consider an automatic start, but his touchdown potential makes him worth keeping in consideration. I’d feel comfortable using him as a flex option this week.
Justin Herbert is usually a quarterback fantasy managers don’t have to think twice about starting. Unfortunately, his performance through the first six games has made that decision a little more complicated.
Herbert has thrown for 1,141 yards with five touchdowns and eight interceptions. Those numbers are nowhere near what fantasy managers expected coming into the season. The Chargers have struggled to find consistency offensively, and Herbert has been unable to produce the type of numbers that make him a dependable fantasy option. Until things start turning around, I’d look at other quarterback options this week.
Ladd McConkey is an interesting option heading into this matchup, especially with his return to the lineup after suffering a concussion.
McConkey has recorded 200 receiving yards and a touchdown this season. His ability to create separation and give Herbert a reliable option underneath makes him an important part of this offense.
However, staying healthy has been a challenge, and the Rams aren’t exactly an easy matchup for opposing receivers. I wouldn’t expect a huge performance immediately, but McConkey is worth considering as a flex option for managers who need help at wide receiver.
Quentin Johnston has shown that he can make big plays, but his involvement in the Chargers offense has been difficult to predict.
He’s recorded 165 receiving yards on eight receptions, averaging an impressive 20.6 yards per catch. The problem is that his opportunities have been limited, making it difficult to trust him on a weekly basis. With Ladd McConkey and Tre’ Harris also available, Johnston could have some competition for targets. He’s capable of making an impact, but I’d rather wait for more consistent involvement before putting him into my starting lineup.
Oronde Gadsden II has shown some promise this season, recording 12 receptions for 103 yards and a touchdown. While those numbers aren’t particularly eye-catching, he has shown that he can contribute when given opportunities.
The biggest question is how consistent his involvement will be moving forward. With Charlie Kolar also in the tight end rotation, Gadsden isn’t necessarily guaranteed the kind of workload fantasy managers need.

title: Why Did The Chargers Opt to Not Fire Mike McDaniel During the Bye Week?
full_text:
Now that the Los Angeles Chargers are heading into Week 8 refreshed from their bye week, it is expected that most teams will come out firing on all cylinders after their week off. However, as a winless team, the Bolts were expected to make drastic coaching-related moves , considering how poor the season has gone.
The team opted to keep everything the same. So that begs the question: why did the Chargers opt to keep Mike McDaniel? Even with the perfect opportunity to fire him?
The Chargers have seemingly always been cursed with poor injury luck and an inability to stay healthy over the course of an NFL season. This year has been more of the same, but coming off their BYE, the team is finding some players back from injury, hopefully giving much-needed 'juice' to one of the league's worst offenses.
Tre Harris, Ladd McConkey, Joe Alt and Branson Taylor are all players who are expected to start (or play an important depth role in Taylor's case) and improve this offense. With the team sputtering early, it could be easy to blame injuries and give McDaniel some more time with an offense that is less banged up.
The Athletic's Chargers beat reporter, Noah Furtado, recently wrote a very insightful article about McDaniel's offense and the learning curve involved with perfecting such a complicated scheme. He interviews players like Daniel Brunskill and Jake Browning as guys who are familiar with the concepts, with both of those individuals giving detail into the complexities and the time it takes to get used to then.
Brunskill, in Furtado's article, mentions: “That takes a little while to get used to, how to run, because when you run you don’t really have a base,” he said. “It took a season. I mean, you learn it by camp and you can run it, but you’re still kind of learning all the ins and outs of it. … The thing with this offense is … that run off the ball is something that you just have to be doing all the time to really get it down.”
With such a complex scheme, could it be possible for the Bolts to liken to the side of patience and give McDaniel and his offense more time to gel?
When someone gets fired, the team obviously needs someone else on staff to take on that role. With head coach Jim Harbaugh never having called plays before, it will fall on someone else in the building. The question would be, who?
The first name that comes most is Adam Gase, former Dolphins and Jets head coach, known for colossal failures during his time as such. His claim to fame is his time as the Broncos' offensive coordinator, helping late-career Peyton Manning achieve success.
Another name could be Shane Day, the Chargers' QB Coach / Passing Game Coordinator. Justin Herbert loves Day, giving an easy path to offensive chemistry, while possibly also giving Herbert some extra 'want' to stick around, considering the team would obviously be doing so to keep him happy.
Even with those two options, it is hard to believe that any of them would be viable candidates to improve the offense, with Day never calling plays at the NFL or college level and Gase not having a strong resume as someone who can make a functional NFL offense in recent memory.
The final part of the equation is McDaniel's contract. It is unknown how much he is being paid, but it is safe to assume that the Chargers spent a pretty penny to get him as their offensive coordinator. He was highly sought after , and usually in those cases, the highest bidder wins.
That said, the Chargers are known as a very "cash-rich" team, making it more difficult to make decisions that require essentially wasting money on coaching.
Overall, it is in everyone's best interest for McDaniel to turn things around. Hopefully, with this belief in him post-bye week, it actually happens.

title: If Mike McDaniel Still has Smashmouth Football in Him, Now is the Time for Chargers
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-6 and their offense has looked lost the entire season. Los Angeles has dealt with significant injuries all season with over half of their initial 53-man roster either on injured reserve or the injury report for week six.
Los Angeles' injury luck started when starting center Tyler Biadasz went down with a significant season-ending knee injury during a joint practice with the 49ers during training camp. The Chargers were forced to shuffle the offensive line with the season less than three weeks away and plug in rookie Jake Slaughter as the new starting center.
The injury to Biadasz seems to have been the catalyst for the wheels falling off of the offense's wagon. We never got to see Biadasz in game action, he did not play any snaps in the first preseason game and was injured before the second. But the reports from that joint practice, before the injury were that the Chargers offense was handily beating up the 49ers. The reports made sense coming on the heels of the Chargers backups physically dominating the Houston Texans in the first preseason game.
"The Chargers, they out-physicaled us the entire game."- Texans head coach Demeco Ryans pic.twitter.com/6Sh456WY3q
Biadasz' going down seems to have been the one injury that the offense and offensive line could not have survived, which raises more questions about roster construction and the interior offensive line as a whole. Regardless, the interior offensive line has not been good. Unfortunately, the injury bug did not stop with the line and attacked the wide receiver room as well.
The Chargers' original six wide receivers have all dealt with injuries this season. Not one of the six has played fully healthy every week and the lack of reps and continuity has ruined the timing of the offense. The disruption in timing paired with a run game that has not been a strong point and consistent interior pressure is largely how the Chargers still have not found their groove on offense.
The past two games before the bye in week seven featured four rookie starting offensive linemen. The Chargers will get Joe Alt back this week at one of the tackle spots, assuming he takes his right tackle spot back. it is possible that second-year lineman Branson Taylor figures somewhere into the lineup but if the lineup remains the same with the exception of Alt's return, the Chargers will still be starting three rookies on the offensive line, the entire left side of the line.
The Chargers rookie offensive linemen have played better than was expected but still have their rookie shortcomings. The good news is tackle Travis Burke and guard Logan Taylor are very capable run blockers. Burke is a mountain of an offensive lineman and generates significant movement at the point of attack. Note Burke's run-blocking grade on the chart below.
OT Percentile Grades in Pass & Run Blocking pic.twitter.com/Qti6mB1CT4
The strengths of the rookies could be the key to getting the Chargers back on track offensively, or at least help them find some sort of rhythm. Los Angeles will be getting some limited reinforcements back as wide receiver Ladd McConkey and Tre Harris are both scheduled to make their returns to the fields this week against the Rams. Tight end Charlie Kolar and wide receiver Quintin Johnston both emergeed from the bye without injury designations.
The question will be how does Mike McDaniel and the Chargers adjust following the bye week? Does McDaniel have any downhill smashmouth football left in his arsenal? The Chargers rushing attack has been much more successful to the left side and between the tackles. Compared to a similar offensive system in San Francisco, the Chargers run the ball between the tackles almost 20 percent less.
Based on EPA or expected points added by personnel groupings, the Chargers most efficient run formations are in 13 personnel lining up with a running back and three tight ends followed closely by  22 personnel featuring two tight ends and a fullback.
The Chargers should line up with Charlie Kolar, Hayden Rucci and Scott Matlock on the field and run right behind Travis Burke or Joe Alt, both of whom have comparable run blocking grades.
The Rams run dime personnel packages on defense nearly 50 percent of the time, meaning they have extra defensive backs on the field and create pressure by rotating and sending different players to the line of scrimmage. If they want to give the Chargers lighter defensive personnel packages, the Chargers should lean into what strengths they have.
The Rams sent most of their starting defensive line to injured reserve. They still have Aaron Donald and he can still wreck an offensive line's gameplan but Myles Garrett will not be back yet so the focus can be on Donald.
The offense under Mike McDaniel has not gone smoothly. There is blame to go around to every corner of the team and organization. But, if the Chargers and McDaniel found positives to lean into coming out the bye, now is the time to implement them.
Based on the available personnel and data from first six weeks, ditching the higher frequency of outside zone in favor of more inside zone or gap runs may be beneficial. It does go against the Miami version of McDaniel, can he tap into his Shanahan roots as a playcaller against the Rams?

title: 6 Winners and 1 Clear Loser in Rams' 24-9 Win Over Chargers
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams beat the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 8, 24-9, to improve to 4-4 on the season. It may not have been perfect, but the second half was another glimpse of what the Rams can be when they put it all together. While the first half was rough, there was a lot to like in the second half. Here are the winners and losers from Sunday’s win against the Chargers.
For a second consecutive week, Blake Corum provided the spark that the Rams' run game needed. In the first half, the Rams had five carries for 10 yards. On the first drive of the second half, Corum had five carries for 55 yards, capped off by a 23-yard touchdown run. Corum finished with 11 carries for 73 yards, and up until the final drive, he was out-carrying Kyren Williams. Corum has been an ‘x-factor’ over the last two weeks and his 23 yards after forcing missed tackles was a season-high.
Really good day for Blake Corum in the run game. Provided spark and energy that the Rams offense and run game lacked in the first half. Via NFL Pro he generated a season-high 23 yards after forcing missed tackles. pic.twitter.com/eAsW6i32y9
Donald still doesn’t have a sack this season, but his impact was felt throughout the game on Sunday. He had a tackle for loss in the run game and consistently made his presence felt. After a Wesley Bailey strip sack, Donald very nearly had a scoop and score for his first career touchdown. Things are starting to click for Donald once again, and it seems like only a matter of time before he finally gets to the quarterback.
Aaron Donald doing Aaron Donald things 😌 LACvsLAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/kBqz4E1udQ
Over the last two weeks, an argument can be made that Omar Speights has been one of the best defenders on the field. He had four impact plays via Sumer Sports, including a tackle for loss. Speights also had a pass breakup in coverage. He was all over the field and, most importantly, had zero missed tackles.
The first half should have been all the evidence that the Rams needed to convince themselves that they should trade for a wide receiver . Outside of Puka Nacua, Tutu Atwell was the only wide receiver with a reception. Nacua caught 11 of his 12 targets, while Atwell, Konata Mumpfield, and Jordan Whittington combined for two catches on six targets. Stafford’s interception came when targeting Mumpfield. It was evident that Stafford was uncomfortable and unsettled when Nacua wasn’t open. Whether it’s Josh Downs or Brian Thomas Jr., the Rams need to make a trade for a wide receiver.
For the first time in two weeks, Trent McDuffie was back on the field for the Rams’ defense and he made his presence felt. McDuffie led the Rams with nine tackles and also had an interception that turned into a touchdown for the offense. Josh Wallace and Emmanuel Forbes have stepped up well in McDuffie’s place. However, Sunday showed why the Rams traded for him. He’s important to the Rams’ success on defense.
There’s a conversation to be had that Wesley Bailey should be getting more snaps in the edge rusher rotation than Josaiah Stewart. Both players had a sack on Sunday against the Chargers, but it’s hard not to come away impressed with Bailey. Bailey stripped Herbert and forced a fumble on his sack, nearly creating a turnover, and was stout in the run game.. For an undrafted free agent, he is exceeding expectations and has become an important piece of the pass rush.
Josh Karty and the dirty kickoff certainly weren’t perfect. It needs to be more consistent as the Rams can’t give teams the ball at the 40-yard line. With that said, when it did work, the Chargers took over at the 23, 28, and 19. That’s better than what the kickoff coverage unit had been doing. It needs work and a better team would take advantage of the opportunity before the half. However, it seems to be a step in the right direction.

title: Rams Overcome Slow Start to Beat Chargers, but Need for Trade Deadline Help Remains
full_text:
One week after the Los Angeles Rams appeared to find their identity, it looked like they had lost it early against the Los Angeles Chargers. In the second half, the Rams stole it back on their way to a 24-9 win.
On the back of the run game and 13 personnel, the Rams finally found some consistency on offense. However, an injury to Colby Parkinson coming into the game on Sunday changed the entire dynamic and it took time for the Rams to adjust.
In the first half, the Rams operated out of 11 personnel on 75 percent of their offensive plays. When the Rams were without Parkinson against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 4, they at least had Nacua and Davante Adams. As the Rams were forced into 11 personnel on Sunday, they were looking at a rotation of Tutu Atwell, Konata Mumpfield, and Jordan Whittington in the passing game.
For the first 28 minutes of the game, the Rams didn’t have a first down. While the offense took advantage of a Quentin Lake interception on Justin Herbert, the Rams’ offense looked broken. Matthew Stafford started the game with an interception and was 6-for-10 for 20 yards until the team’s final drive of the opening half. Stafford didn’t seem comfortable throwing to any wide receiver not named Nacua.
If the Rams needed evidence that they needed to trade for a wide receiver , Sunday certainly provided that. While Nacua caught 11-of-12 targets, Mumpfield, Atwell and Jordan Whittington combined for 2-for-7. Nacua finished with 80 of Stafford’s 157 yards on the day.
Sunday marked the first time in the Sean McVay era that the Rams went their first five offensive drives without a first down. The Rams had 14 yards on their first five drives of the game.
Finally, with less than two minutes to go in the half, the offense got going. Stafford found Tutu Atwell for a gain of 40 yards deep down the left sideline for the team’s first first down of the half, and then hit Nacua open over the middle to set the offense up at the two-yard line. On the next play, Kyren Williams walked into the end zone to give the Rams a 10-9 lead.
After getting away from the run game in the first half and running the ball just five times, the Rams came out with a mission on their opening drive of the third quarter. Blake Corum carried the ball four straight times for 32 yards to spark the run game . Corum then capped the drive off with a 23-yard touchdown run, putting the Rams ahead 17-9.
The Rams made it a point to get back to the same rushing identity that they established last week. In the first half, the Rams ran the ball five times for just 10 yards. Corum and Williams combined for 22 carries for 119 yards in the second half. Both players rushed for a touchdown for a third time this season.
While the offense struggled at times throughout the afternoon, the Rams’ defense remained rock solid. Lake had an interception in the first half and the defense didn’t allow a single touchdown for the second time in three weeks.
Back in the lineup, Trent McDuffie intercepted Herbert in the third quarter to give the offense good field position. The Rams took advantage and took a 24-9 lead as Stafford found Nacua on a back-side screen, and Nacua did the rest.
As the Chargers made a final push in the fourth quarter, Josh Wallace tackled tight end Orande Gadsden one-yard short on 4th-and-8 to force a turnover on downs. The Rams then ran Williams 11 times on the next drive to close out the game.
It certainly wasn’t perfect, but the Rams responded in the second half and the offense did enough when it needed to. For the first time this season, the Rams got back-to-back wins. Coming into the game, the main goal was to find a way to start stacking wins and the Rams did just that. They are now back at .500 before they travel to Washington next week to take on the Commanders.
Through eight games, the Rams have yet to play a complete game and find their stride. However, earning a second straight win is a step in the right direction. Now, the Rams need to build on their current momentum and show that the last two weeks are the beginning of something more.

title: Why a Jonathan Taylor Trade Could Complicate Rams' Pursuit of Josh Downs
full_text:
As the NFL trade deadline approaches, one name the Los Angeles Rams have been connected to is Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Josh Downs . After the Colts traded franchise cornerstone Quenton Nelson and defensive lineman DeForest Buckner earlier this week, the team officially entered a fire sale. While the team was already fielding calls on Downs, he officially requested a trade. Running back Jonathan Taylor was initially thought to not be available, but trade talks around him have begun to heat up as well.
With Downs reportedly available, the Rams have a prime opportunity to address one of their biggest roster needs at an affordable price. However, if the Colts were to trade Taylor, it could significantly complicate those plans.
There’s no doubt that the Colts are looking to trade players who may not have a future on the team. However, there comes a point when the Colts can only trade so many players before they are no longer competitive. If the Colts trade one, it seems unlikely they would trade the other. Given the haul that the Colts could get in return for Taylor to use in their upcoming rebuild, he may be the preferred option.
Trading Downs even before moving on from Taylor is complicated for the Colts. According to ESPN’s Stephen Holder, the Colts value Downs at a third-round pick and would prefer to keep him. This offseason, the Colts signed Alec Pierce to a large contract, but he’s currently on injured reserve and has been hurt most of the year.
If the Colts were to trade Downs, it would leave them with Keenan Allen, Laquon Treadwell, and Ashton Dulin at wide receiver. Moving on from Taylor and Downs would give the Colts almost no offensive weapons outside of Tyler Warren.
As I noted last week, if the Rams wanted to trade for Downs, they needed to move quickly . Not only was the wide receiver market heating up, but there was always the possibility of the situation changing. The Colts are currently in fire-sale mode, but they won’t stay there forever.
The Colts may be prioritizing the future, but they still need to be able to field a competitive offense to be able to evaluate the players still on the roster. Trading Taylor would already take away the focal point of the offense, and trading Downs would leave them with very little to work with, especially with Pierce injured
This creates a dilemma for the Rams and general manager Les Snead. They could wait until closer to the deadline and for the wide receiver market to take shape. However, waiting also risks the Colts making another blockbuster move by trading Taylor, which could effectively take Downs off the market.
At 25 years old, Downs could be seen as someone the Colts can build a receiver room around when they are ready to compete again. It’s possible that the Colts decide that keeping Downs and trying to extend him this offseason or taking a future compensatory pick is more beneficial than moving him for just a mid-round selection in next year’s draft.
While the Colts were willing to move on from Nelson and Buckner, they may be more reluctant to trade Taylor and Downs. In 2022, the 49ers traded second-, third-, fourth- and fifth-round picks to the Carolina Panthers for running back Christian McCaffrey. That’s a lot more than what the Colts will get for Downs and will give them more assets to help their rebuild.
If the Rams want Downs , they may need to make their move before the Colts make a decision on Taylor. Waiting for the market to settle is typically smart, but in this case, it could cost the Rams an opportunity before the trade deadline. If the Colts decide to trade Taylor, it could change their priorities and make a deal for Downs much more difficult.
