title: Why Chasing Jonathan Taylor Wouldn't Be a Repeat of the Giants’ 2022 Mistake
full_text:
The New York Giants ’ reported trade interest in big names such as former Titans defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons (now with the Bears) and Colts running back Jonathan Taylor has the fan base and the football world in general abuzz.
But Ted Nguyen of The Athletic views the Giants’ reported push to be big-time buyers in the final days before the Nov. 10 trade deadline as recent Big Blue history repeating itself, and not in a good way.
The film analyst, taking to X , wrote, “Giants going after Jonathan Taylor is a classic team that’s ‘ahead of schedule’ mistake, IMO.
“Harbaugh had (sic) made a difference, and they are competing every week, but do they really think they are an RB away from being a true contender?”
Taylor, the Colts' second-round pick in 2020, has earned first-team All-Pro honors (2021), three Pro Bowl selections (2021, 2024 and 2025), one league rushing yardage title (2021) and two league rushing touchdown titles (2021 and 2025). Indianapolis is now reportedly open to trading him .
The 27-year-old Taylor is signed through 2028, and he represents the type of bell cow running back Giants head coach John Harbaugh wistfully wished for just two weeks ago.
NFL insider Tom Pelissero reported that the Colts rejected a 2027 second-round draft pick plus an additional pick for the running back, suggesting they believe some desperate team looking for a bell cow might do whatever it takes to acquire him.
The crux of Nguyen’s objection seems to be the mistake the Giants made after the 2022 season. Following a 9-7-1 campaign that included a postseason berth, the team went backward because general manager Joe Schoen thought it was further along than it really was.
In retrospect, that 2022 team never really had a clear identity, as the roster-building process felt like the front office was merely slapping pieces together at random.
That hasn’t been the case with the 2026 team, which has a clear identity on both sides of the ball. As a result, it has been easier for the front office to add players who fit Harbaugh’s vision and get rid of those who don’t.
The result has been a Giants team that, while not always pretty, has been competitive. Say what you want about the quality of the NFC East, which has come into focus as the season has gone on.
Harbaugh has still kept the team competitive and within the identity he envisioned, despite losing his starting quarterback and outside linebacker, which speaks to a lack of panic when adversity has hit.
Harbaugh and the Giants have seemingly taken the approach of swapping draft picks for players who not only fit their vision and identity but are also under contract for multiple years.
Those in favor of building through the draft might argue that the approach is akin to cutting corners. What they ignore is that the Giants’ attempts to rebuild via the draft have not exactly been at the top of the league in terms of success, and that Harbaugh isn’t willing to wait until the team is two or three draft classes into his tenure to make a run.
Acquiring Taylor, if the Giants can do so, would fit a major piece of the puzzle into an existing framework rather than trying to reinvent the wheel, as might have been the case in 2022.
The most important thing to remember is that such a move, if it comes to fruition, is less about the short term than the big picture. And while Nguyen also argues that “[Taylor] should be for a contender trying to go over the top,” well, isn’t that what the Giants are trying to do?

title: 4 College Prospects Giants Scouts Should Watch This Weekend
full_text:
As the New York Giants enjoy their much-needed bye week, Giants scouts may be watching closely as college football’s Week 9 slate unfolds.
With the stretch run ahead at 4-2-1, this could be a good time to scout potential targets as prospects make their cases for selection in the 2027 NFL Draft.
Beyond running back, the team’s biggest need remains defensive tackle. Coach John Harbaugh and his staff may also want to keep an eye on late Day 3 or undrafted options in the kicking game, should rookie Dominic Zvada’s struggles continue.
Here are four players the Giants may watch this weekend.
Despite Cam Skattebo’s stellar Week 7 performance against the Houston Texans, New York is still likely to be in the market for a running back this draft season.
Though the position may no longer be Big Blue’s top priority, the team may be wise to take a close look at Florida’s Jadan Baugh, the consensus top running back in this year’s draft class.
The 6-foot-1, 225-pound back is a well-built rusher who can be effective on every down. In addition to his impressive blend of size and speed, Baugh is known for his impeccable ball security.
Aside from one fumble during his freshman season, the Atlanta native has held onto the ball for more than 1,000 collegiate snaps. Given the Giants’ struggles with ball security this season, Baugh would likely put those concerns to rest.
In a marquee matchup against No. 3 Georgia this weekend, Baugh should be well-motivated to add to his 763 rushing yards and 13 rushing touchdowns. He has also caught nine passes for 59 yards out of the backfield.
While the Giants continue to be linked to defensive tackle trade rumors as the NFL’s Nov. 10 deadline approaches, they may find a few college prospects quite intriguing. Washington deserves to be on that list, largely because he can play anywhere along the defensive front.
At 6-foot-3 and 330 pounds, the Detroit native has impressive size and power, with much of that potential still untapped.
Washington is at his best when stacking blockers, while using his frame to anchor and resist opposing double teams. As a run defender, he projects to maintain gap integrity at the pro level.
As the Ducks prepare to face No. 20 Northwestern in Week 9, look for Washington to be a factor in run defense while showcasing his surprisingly quick first step when trying to collapse the pocket.
As a former defensive end, Etta is well-versed in getting after the quarterback off the edge and finishing rushes with sacks. However, his versatility in taking on double teams and stuffing run plays led the Wolverines to move him inside.
Given the Giants’ need for an ominous presence on the interior of their defensive line, Etta could be an intriguing fit. He has developed as a run defender, and he uses both his athleticism and technique to pressure the quarterback.
On that note, the Giants may be wise to keep an eye on SHI Stadium in nearby Piscataway, N.J., as Michigan takes on Rutgers this weekend, especially with Etta determined to add to his 20 tackles and 0.5 sacks for the Wolverines this season.
Although teams rarely invest draft capital in specialists, Carneiro is among the top kicking prospects in this year’s class. With Zvada’s recent struggles, New York might wish to keep its options open heading into 2027.
Since transferring to Ole Miss from Western Kentucky following the 2024 season, Carneiro has become one of the Rebels’ top point-scoring weapons.
The 5-foot-11, 195-pounder is known for his leg strength and clutch kicking. His 48-yard game-winner against Louisville on Sept. 6 earned him co-winner honors for the SEC Special Teams Player of the Week award.
This season, the Cornelius, N.C., native has made 11 of 14 field goals, with his longest coming on a 57-yarder against Charlotte in Week 2. Carneiro has also been perfect on extra-point attempts, going 29-for-29 and earning a total of 62 points.
In what many expect to be a closely contested matchup against Auburn, Carneiro may get a few chances to showcase his kicking prowess this weekend.

title: Harbaugh’s Trade Plan for the Giants Comes Into Focus
full_text:
The New York Giants are enjoying a renaissance under head coach John Harbaugh. They not only sit atop the NFC East with a 4-2-1 record but are also assured of remaining there despite having their bye this week.
Harbaugh, for his part, wants to make sure the Giants stay in first place, so much so that a report from The Athletic claims the 64-year-old head coach took the initiative and made a direct call to Titans controlling owner Amy Adams Strunk regarding defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons.
Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick were ultimately traded by the Titans to Chicago in exchange for first-round picks in 2027 and 2028, and a 2027 fourth-round pick.
It shows that Harbaugh, who, remember, does not report to general manager Joe Schoen but instead reports directly to team ownership, isn’t playing around or waiting, and that he will do everything possible to ensure he gets what he wants for the team.
The fact that Harbaugh reached out to the Titans directly is telling. Such aggressive moves, made at the expense of the team’s draft assets, suggest the roster, while solid, still has multiple glaring holes for Harbaugh and his goal of getting the Giants over the finish line in first place.
As a result, rather than sitting back and investing in young talent via the 2027 draft, which may or may not work out and won’t help them win the division in 2026, he has chosen to be proactive and aggressive in acquiring players who are not only established but also under contract for multiple years.
It’s a sharp change of direction from the patient “build via the draft” approach the organization has used for years, one that produced far too many swings and misses.
Had the Giants been able to land Simmons, they would have had arguably one of the best and most established defensive tackles in football under contract through 2030, which to put into perspective is roughly the length of a first-round pick’s rookie contract with the fifth-year option exercised.
This is the same approach the Giants are reportedly taking with Taylor, the 27-year-old 2021 league rushing leader and three-time Pro Bowler, who, per ESPN, is now on the trade block .
Taylor, a 2020 second-rounder, is under contract through 2028, one year shy of the standard four-year rookie deal typically given to a Day 2 draft pick.
With the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline coming up, it would not be surprising if the Giants go all out to give Harbaugh the running back he wants. He recently shared some insight into how he views the position.
“I would love for us to be in that kind of a circumstance — a Derrick Henry circumstance or a Saquon Barkley circumstance, or whatever it might be,” he told reporters after being asked about the sudden release of running back Najee Harris. “That would be great.”
With no defensive tackles believed to be available via trade who might warrant the kind of haul the Titans got for Simmons, it will be interesting to see whether the Giants can work with the Colts to give Harbaugh his wish.

title: Giants Mailbag: Cam Skattebo, Trading for a Running Back and More
full_text:
Welcome to the weekly New York Giants On SI mailbag! From offseason moves to game-day strategies, we'll do our best to answer your questions. (Some questions have been edited for brevity and clarity.)
Is Cam Skattebo the Giants solidified RB1? I feel he is the Giants best RB, regardless of the ball security problem.
Technically, no. By definition, an RB1, or “bell cow,” is an every-down player who handles most rushing and receiving touches, as opposed to someone who is part of a committee.
When I think of a RB1, I think of Derrick Henry of Baltimore, Jonathan Taylor of Indy, Jahmyr Gibbs of Detroit, Bijan Robinson of Atlanta, and Kenneth Walker III of Kansas City.  All of those guys I mentioned have played in at least 80% of their team’s offensive snaps.
Skattebo? He’s only played in 47.1% of the Giants' offensive snaps, as he’s been part of a committee — and had he not served a quasi-benching in Week 6, it wouldn’t have made a difference.
So by that definition, no, Skattebo is not an RB1. Is he the Giants’ RB1? Yes. But is he an NFL RB1? No.
What is more realistic, trading for a top RB like Taylor, a mid RB like Pollard, a vet RB to share the load, or no trade a tall? #askPTrain
Mike, I still do not think the Giants are going to trade for a running back. Again, I will die on the hill because, given the inconsistency of the run defense, in my opinion, they have to acquire a big-bodied plugger for their defensive line, and that is the move that should be prioritized.
Let’s dig a bit into history. The last time the Giants traded in-season for a running back was back in October 1986 when they acquired Ottis Anderson from the then St. Louis Cardinals. They felt they were a player away from making a run and sure enough, Anderson helped them accomplish that.
More recently, let’s look at John Harbaugh’s history with Baltimore. In 2020, the Ravens spent a second-round pick on J.K. Dobbins, and in 2008, the Ravens used a second-round pick on Ray Rice. Those were the only two times the Ravens, with Harbaugh as head coach, spent that high of a draft asset on a running back.
Now maybe the Giants would have drafted Jeremiyah Love in the first round this year, but we’ll never know for sure. My point is I can’t see the Giants parting with premium assets like a Day 1 or Day 2 draft pick for a running back when they’re not one running back away from making a run.
Good morning Pat!  During the bye week, what is one improvement on each side of the ball you would look to make?  I like Mooney, but I feel like if we can get someone like Josh Downs from Indy, that would be an upgrade. I would also look to add some DL help. #askPTrain
Hi KDF. I covered it in this article . I’ve been screaming for D-line help, but I suspect it won’t come until the draft next year. Still, we have been covering various options here and here .
I do agree with you about Darnell Mooney. He’s a low-cost option, but I sense Malachi Fields has passed him up on the depth chart and in terms of production.
Had an idea.  I want the Giants to retire 53 but it won’t happen.  What if it was given as an honor to the captain of the defense.  Someone like Burns after he earns it.
What’s good, Kris? That’s a nice idea, but it can’t happen in a game. Remember, rules still govern which jersey numbers certain positions can wear. What happens if a quarterback, running back, tight end, or receiver earns the right to wear it? Again, per the jersey numbering rules, that can’t happen.
Now, if you wanted to give the number to a deserving player to wear in practice, I don't believe any rule prohibits that. But not in a game. (Besides, I think Burns is pretty happy wearing zero.)
Do you think Harbaugh will call plays to keep Zvada off the right hash going  forward on FGs until he gets a few consecutive makes under his belt?
It doesn't exactly work that way, Jeff. The hash for a field goal attempt depends on where the previous play ended. If you intentionally run third-down plays to one side when you reach field goal range, teams will notice, and you'll become predictable.
The bottom line is that Zvada needs to learn to kick from both hashes.
Are there any options in Free Agency that you would want the Giants to go after? Just one year deals that can help us remain competitive for this season. Nothing that will hurt us financially in the future. #askPTrain
Do you mean street free agents? If so, the only one that intrigues me is defensive tackle Austin Johnson. If you mean free agents in the future, then it’s way too early for that discussion.

title: Bold Trade Idea for Giants: Cash In on John Michael Schmitz Before the Deadline
full_text:
If nothing else, the New York Giants have proven that they’re not afraid to shake up the roster, especially with their eyes firmly on winning the NFC East.
And with the league’s trade deadline fast approaching, there’s been plenty of talk about who the Giants might acquire, but little about who, if anyone, they might move to recoup draft picks.
So here’s a thought about the latter: Why not see if the Green Bay Packers would be interested in acquiring center John Michael Schmitz in exchange for a draft pick?
Crazy, you say? Perhaps. But let’s explore this wild scenario anyway.
Simple. Injuries have hit their offensive line hard. They are already on their third center this season after losing Sean Rhyan, their Week 1 starter, to a high ankle sprain in Week 7 and backup Jacob Monk to a quad injury that same week.
Rhyan is expected to miss between four and six weeks . Right now, the Packers are down to John Williams, their seventh-round pick in 2025, who stepped in for Monk against the Detroit Lions last week.
Per PFF , Monk has allowed 11 pressures this season, and Williams has allowed five. Is it that hard to believe the Packers would want a better option at center moving forward, as they also fight to win their division?
Why not? It’s obvious that after losing his starting job to Bryan Hudson back in Week 4, Schmitz, who, by the way, is in the final year of his rookie contract, isn’t in the long-term plans for the Giants.
Rather than let him walk in the 2027 free agency cycle and risk getting nothing in return, why not see if the team can get a draft pick for him from a club in need, such as the Packers?
Doing so not only guarantees a 2027 pick, but also adds to a haul that already includes five picks, plus a potential extra fourth-round pick projected to come the Giants’ way via the compensatory system.
If the Giants can get extra picks for players who don’t have a long-term future with the team, why not pursue that avenue?
To win now. If Green Bay isn’t happy with its current center situation, it makes the upgrade now and worries later about whether anyone on an expiring contract will be back.
And let’s say, for argument’s sake, that the Giants and Packers made this trade. Would it be a rental? Probably. But remember, the Packers signed Rhyan to a three-year, $33 million contract in March of this year, so it's probably safe to say that he’s their starter moving forward.
And Schmitz? Since he’s in the final year of his rookie deal, he’d cost the Packers approximately $230,823 for each week he’s on the roster, which isn’t a huge financial strain for a team that currently has $6.422 million in salary cap space.
Per Tankathon , the Packers are projected to have 11 draft picks in 2027. That haul includes two fourth-round picks, three fifth-round picks (two of which are projected compensatory picks), and two sixth-round picks (one compensatory pick).
If the Packers are desperate for an upgrade at center, would anyone balk at trading a fifth-round pick for a center who was a second-round pick in his draft class?
Currently, Schmitz is listed as Hudson’s backup after losing his starting job, meaning there is no other center on the roster at the moment.
But the Giants do have a couple of players on the practice squad who could be options for promotion to the 53-man roster if the team moves on from Schmitz via a trade.
The most obvious is Kendrick Green, a veteran who has been in the NFL since 2021 and has played 975 snaps at center , most recently in 2024 with Houston.
Green also spent the 2025 season in Cleveland with Giants offensive line coach Mike Bloomgren, so he is probably already ahead of the curve in adapting to the techniques Bloomgren teaches.
Another option would be Lodi, N.J. native Geno VanDeMark. VanDeMark is still a young player looking to get his NFL footing, but he played 161 snaps at center over his college career at both Michigan State and Alabama.

title: Jets Week 8 Report Card: Grading Every Position After 2nd-Half Collapse vs. Raiders
full_text:
After blowing an opportunity against the previously winless Dolphins in Week 7, it only got worse for the Jets after getting outscored, 24-10, in the second half and losing a 38-33 shootout to the Raiders on Sunday in the second of back-to-back home games.
It was a much quicker start for the Jets with points on all five of their first-half drives. They even outgained the Raiders, 439-333, and were about as efficient as you could ask for offensively, but the persistent red-zone issues (2-of-6), poor special teams play and the defense's inability to get consistent stops proved costly in a tightly contested game.
Instead of winning a pair of games on home soil at MetLife Stadium, the Jets lost both and head into a trickier part of the schedule riding their second three-game losing streak in just eight games with a disappointing 2-6 record.
Before we get too far ahead to a Week 9 road trip to Arrowhead Stadium to face the Chiefs, let's hand out some grades for each unit following another blown opportunity against the Raiders.
Geno Smith was instrumental in New York's quicker start and efficient offensive performance. He was 20-of-32 for 290 yards with two touchdowns and one interception, averaging a solid 9.1 yards per attempt and pushing the ball downfield effectively as the Jets went on to score on each of the offense's first six possessions.
It was not a perfect performance for Smith against his former team, but he ended the game on a sour note with the game-ending interception on Gang Green's final drive as Jeremy Chinn came down with the toe-tapping pick in the end zone .
Jeremy Chinn seals the victory for the Raiders and shows off some toe drag swag for the INT off Geno Smith. pic.twitter.com/Eqd8TQpAH4
The long-awaited breakout performance finally came from WR Adonai Mitchell, coming off zero catches on three targets in his return from a finger injury. He led the way for the Jets' passing attack with seven catches (on nine targets) for 142 yards and a 12-yard touchdown that gave the game its fourth lead change of the opening half.
Garrett Wilson was finally a bigger part of the offense with six catches (on 12 targets) for 83 yards, while Isaiah Williams scored the first TD of the game for Gang Green after a slow start to the season. Rookie Omar Cooper Jr. was not a factor after back-to-back 100-yard receiving games, but it is clear this is a talented group of wideouts where any of the three starters can go off on any given Sunday.
One week after Mason Taylor exploded for two TDs and had a career outing for himself, the TE group made little impact this week. Rookie Kenyon Sadiq had one reception for 22 yards and Taylor came down with three of his five targets for 19 yards, but it was clear the focus this week was more on the WR unit and distributing the ball on the outside against a Raiders defense that ranks 29th in the league in points allowed (28.1 ppg).
It was still some complementary football from this group alongside the wideouts and they helped stretch the middle of the field, but they did not have an impactful performance this time around. It only made matters worse that Raiders TE Brock Bowers went for 92 yards and two TDs and completely took over the game for his unit.
It was hard to find much to be disappointed with from this group as Braelon Allen went off for 21 carries, 147 yards and one TD, averaging a career-high seven yards per carry in the process. He broke free for this 21-yard TD run to give the Jets a nine-point lead in the third quarter (h/t NFL).
Braelon Allen scores and now has 142 rushing yards on the day! LVvsNYJ on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/aGaC9Th33s
He is the first Jets running back with three straight 100-yard games since Hall of Famer Curtis Martin and continues to do a phenomenal job filling in for the injured Breece Hall. Isaiah Davis only had five carries for 15 yards, but he did not have to do much, as Allen completely dominated the Raiders up front and gave the offense some explosive plays to balance out the pass game.
Although they were not as dominant in the second half, the O-line continues to show glimpses of how effective it can be in the trenches. In addition to affording Smith plenty of time to throw, Allen had his way on the ground and took advantage of some open lanes to make the Raiders pay on numerous occasions.
They did allow two sacks and failed to capitalize late with some penalties and an inability to finish out drives when the end zone was in sight. That said, starting left guard Dylan Parham returned to the lineup and was instrumental in helping the unit up front open up holes for Allen to exploit, and it was clear what potential exists as this unit takes more snaps together.
Despite an uncertain future surrounding Will McDonald IV , he recorded his third sack of the season late in the first quarter (h/t SNY Jets) and provided a bright spot for a D-line that was without four of its starters for Sunday's game.
Will McDonald gets the third-down sack 💪 pic.twitter.com/OatTNNgtsD
That was even followed by a fourth-down stop on the Raiders' next offensive possession, but it was clear this unit was banged up and struggling to contain anything Las Vegas threw at them. Granted, the Raiders only mustered 95 yards on the ground, but the Jets could not find a way to slow down QB Kirk Cousins and could not get off the field on third down, as the problems only seem to be getting worse up front as the injuries keep piling up.
Jamien Sherwood continued his breakout season with a team-high 14 tackles (five solo) while also being active against the run. Demario Davis was not bad, either, with seven tackles (one solo), but this unit was still a mixed bag that failed to provide much relief from the inconsistency up front on the D-line.
Coverage issues were a clear problem, with Bowers going off for a pair of TDs and RB Ashton Jeanty going for 64 yards on just three receptions. The inability to contain the open field and limit Bowers and Jeanty proved costly, as did the critical conversions that were allowed in the second half.
The Jets have utilized a heavy dose of man coverage this season, and this was one of the key matchups entering the weekend to see how the secondary could fare against Bowers. Coverage breakdowns and communication issues were prevalent throughout the game as Bowers had his way, and Cousins completed 19 of 26 passes for 247 yards and three TDs, in addition to a season-best 141.0 passer rating.
The secondary failed to create a game-changing takeaway and, while safety Dane Belton led the group with 12 tackles (nine solo), along with one tackle for loss and one pass defended, it was a struggle for the entire group. That was particularly true for Brandon Stephens, who continues to become an unnecessary Jets headache after being called for a defensive holding penalty on a third-and-goal in the third quarter, which led to a Raiders TD a few plays later.
This has nothing to do with kicker Jason Sanders, who nailed all four of his field goals and each of his three extra points. Punter Austin McNamara was solid with an average of 44 yards per punt, and Williams averaged 33 yards on both kickoff returns, but the 95-yard kickoff-return TD from Dylan Laube (h/t NFL+) was the difference in the game.
✅ 95 yards to the house ✅ Raiders' first kickoff return since 2011 ✅ NFL's first kick return TD of 2026 ✅ Dylan Laube's fastest TD (20.97 MPH via @NextGenStats ) LVvsNYJ on FOX/FOX One Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/xu0hAbc4RK
Simply put, that type of play cannot happen, especially in a game decided by five points. You can point to the D-line's continued struggles and some more coaching miscues from this staff, but that play completely flipped the momentum and had a huge say in the outcome of the game, even if the rest of the special teams unit held up its end of the bargain.

title: Biggest Jets Studs & Duds in Week 8 Loss to Raiders: Aaron Glenn's Superpowers Fail on Braelon Allen's Big Day
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Where were you when the Jets' offense exploded to one of their most impressive performances over the last decade?
Where were you when the Jets' best offensive performance was squandered by a poor defense and special teams breakdowns?
New York scored on their first six drives of the game to kick off Week 8 , but it wasn't enough. The Las Vegas Raiders, encouraged by a large traveling fanbase, took control of the contest late and held on for the 38-33 win. The loss dropped the Jets to a 2-6 mark in a game where they had over 400 yards of offense and over 166 yards on the ground.
As with any loss, there are studs and duds from Sunday's game. Let's break them all down right now.
We have come to the point now where Braelon Allen's production has far exceeded anything a single Jets running back has done since Hall of Famer Curtis Martin was with the team in 2004. Allen ran for 147 yards on 21 carries, including a 21-yard touchdown run to give New York a two-score lead into the third quarter.
Braelon Allen scores and now has 142 rushing yards on the day! LVvsNYJ on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/aGaC9Th33s
Allen became the first running back in team history to have three straight 100-yard games on the ground since Martin. He has become the bell cow that many Jets fans have hoped to see from Breece Hall.
After the game, head coach Aaron Glenn talked about Allen's performance and focused on not rushing Hall back from his quad injury.
At the end of the day, though, the Jets cannot move Allen away from the starting lineup . He has been too dominant to stop.
New York's offense had its most dominant day of yard production we have seen in quite some time. The unit recorded 424 yards of offense, including 166 on the ground. The problem, though, lay in the fact that the red zone offense was an abysmal 2-for-6 .
Four field goals kicked and only two touchdowns. Unacceptable in the modern age of offense-first football.
There were many issues why the unit struggled. Sometimes, like in the game's opening drive, the team couldn't hook up with their best players. Garrett Wilson couldn't corral a back-shoulder fade. Later in the game, though, penalties and missed throws all played a role.
No team that puts up 33 points should lose a game in the NFL. New York's offense will have a lot they can be happy about today.
But the Jets also could have put the game out of reach multiple times and failed to do so. When their defense eventually broke, they didn't have an answer.
New York's starting quarterback was not perfect on Sunday. He missed several throws early on and threw a pick to end the game instead of giving his offense one more chance to score on a Hail Mary.
But those mistakes aside, Smith was excellent for the Jets all game. He finished 20-for-32 passing for two touchdowns and the late pick. He was sacked twice in the second half but repeatedly pushed the ball downfield against Las Vegas' maligned secondary.
One thing Smith will want back is the team's red zone success; we'll get to that later. But putting up 33 points should be enough to win a game in the NFL. Smith's performance, again, was good enough to win.
Last season, the Jets rostered one of the best special teams units of all time. Before 2026 began, there was major concern about how Jason Sanders would look, but genuine confidence was found in their unit as a whole.
Things have changed drastically since the start of the season, though.
New York gave up a 95-yard touchdown return in the first half that gave Las Vegas the lead, 14-13. For a game that was decided by one score, the special teams breakdown was a game-turning play. It won't matter that Sanders made all four of his field goals today either.
It will be remembered for the breakdown in coverage that gave Las Vegas seven free points.
The second half wasn't as dominant as the first, but the Jets' offensive line continues to play exceptionally well over the last several weeks. New York gave Smith plenty of time to throw and averaged over six yards per carry as a collective unit.
This was also the first game back for starting left guard Dylan Parham. His return brought the group back to a dominant fold. They moved Las Vegas at the line of scrimmage all game and found ways to open holes for whoever was touching the football.
This is a kind of loss that will sting because this group continues to show how good they can be with more snaps together. The future is very bright for New York's offensive line.
New York's defensive line made two nice plays on Sunday.
Throughout the game, though, and particularly in the second half, the Jets' defensive line got tossed around. There's a reason for that, of course. New York was without four starters: David Bailey, David Onyemata, T'Vondre Sweat and Joseph Ossai.
The numbers tell one story. New York gave up just 2.9 yards on the ground in a clear focus of stopping the run, but the team failed to record much pressure at all on Kirk Cousins. That led to 24 points scored in the second half and three straight scoring drives.
The Jets' defensive line is their biggest weakness right now, and it seems like it's only going to get worse.
Fans were waiting to see a breakout performance from AD Mitchell all year. They finally got it on Sunday.
Mitchell caught seven passes for 142 yards and a touchdown. He could have had even more with one drop down the field costing him at least another 42 yards of offense. Mitchell was Smith's most trusted target, as has been the case all season.
An incredible 48-yard catch by Adonai Mitchell! 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/a7pOlkJn27
His development is also huge for a Jets offense that seemed to get Garrett Wilson going (team-high 12 targets), and didn't target rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. The Jets have an embarrassment of riches at receiver now, and it makes their offense very fun to watch.
Even after a loss such as this.
Glenn was clear he wanted to call plays this season because play calling was his "superpower."
It was anything but in Week 8.
Glenn's defense gave up three straight touchdown drives to open up the second half, erasing what had been a 10-point halftime lead into a five-point deficit late in the fourth quarter. Now, a lot of things are working against Glenn. His ideal defensive line is hurt, and the team didn't get the kind of quality play they normally saw from their secondary.
But there were many strategic decisions Glenn made that hurt the team as well. Chief among them was keeping cornerbacks on Las Vegas's tight ends for a majority of the game. Both of Brock Bowers's touchdowns came against cornerbacks. Michael Mayer also made four catches for 46 yards as well.
New York needed a better defensive coaching plan. Especially from someone who was brazen enough to call it his superpower at the start of the offseason.

title: Jets Shouldn't Give Up on Breece Hall Just Yet Despite Breakout Run from Braelon Allen
full_text:
Football fandom is a roller coaster of a run. Sometimes fans become so enamored with a player that they become part of the very fabric of an organization. But when that player struggles or gets hurt, his replacement can sometimes be more beloved than the original star.
That's what might be happening with the New York Jets and their running back room.
For the better part of the last four seasons, Breece Hall has been the feature running back to their offense. The second-round pick out of Iowa State has rushed for over 3,400 yards, and 18 touchdowns while also being one of the best pass catchers at his position. But a quad injury has cost him the last four weeks.
And since, Braelon Allen has taken control of the rushing offense for New York. Now, Jets fans are wondering if the team should move on from their once star running back.
But as Allen's success has grown, that doesn't mean the Jets should be willing to move on from a player they just gave an extension to.
It's easy to say the Jets should move on from Hall after the recent stretch of breakout performances from Allen. The former fourth-round pick is still only 22 years old, and has rushed for nearly 300 yards in the last three games combined. Allen has become the ideal power running back that the Jets had hoped for when they drafted him three years ago.
Continuing to ride the hot hand of Allen makes plenty of sense, even when Hall returns from his injury.
But that doesn't mean Hall is any less impactful. New York has wanted to run a by-committee approach to their running back room since head coach Aaron Glenn was brought into the fold last year.
"We have three running backs on this team that we’re going to utilize as much as possible," Glenn said. "They’re all big men. They can run. They’re violent. They’re physical."
New York shouldn't give up on Hall because of his injuries, nor because Allen is having an incredible run. If the Jets were to trade Hall, it would be the second straight season in which the Jets traded away a player they were high enough on to give a long-term extension. That kind of change may be easy for fans to move past, but it isn't for players. What player would want to get an extension from New York
Furthermore, while Allen's recent run of excellent play should be commended, he has yet to do so for a full 17-game season. To expect his run to continue, as teams begin to see him as a full-time back is not something the Jets should be able to project. It is better for New York to split their touches for their running back room going forward when Hall is healthy, than to depart with one of their runners for the sake of giving Allen more to work with.
Of course, whatever the Jets determine, the team has a truth about their running game that they'll have to deal with going forward.
Quality running backs are a dime a dozen in the NFL. When an offense has a good line, any running back can find success. In the case of the Jets, their line isn't among the elites in the game, but that doesn't make their collection of runners either.
The reality for both Hall and Allen is that neither player is a top-five performer at his position, regardless of the excellent run that Allen is on. Because of this, New York is best served using both together and forcing opposing defenses to prepare for both.
With Hall and Allen on the field, New York could have a run-first component to their scheme, while also putting Hall out as a receiver to confuse defenses as well. If he were to be traded, though, then that creative advantage would be gone before the Jets even had a chance to use it.
It's easy to say that Allen has replaced Hall as New York's starting running back. But the creativity that could come with both on the field is far greater than anything the Jets may have previously had planned.

title: 3 Jets Decisions Have Come Back to Haunt Them by Halloween
full_text:
It's easy to point to several different factors into why the New York Jets find themselves at 2-5.
Poor coaching, inept player execution, and whiffed offseason additions have all played a part to where the team is today. In the case of New York's offseason misses, there were three that have directly impacted their chances of success.
Today, we'll break down the biggest offseason mistakes the Jets made, and how each one has plagued the roster in 2026.
New York's biggest weakness last season was in their run defense. Head coach Aaron Glenn watched his front seven get gashed as the fourth-worst unit in the league. To fix those issues, the Jets and general manager Darren Mougey moved quickly.
Veterans like David Onyemata and T'Vondre Sweat were added at the start of the offseason. New York also drafted David Bailey and Darrell Jackson Jr. to aid their defensive line. The thought behind these moves was that the team would bring in personnel to directly aid in stopping the run.
But what New York actually did was simply overcompensate in the team's weakness. Sweat and Onyemata were run-centric defensive tackles. They did not have a deep history in rushing the passer.
Because of that, the team's pass rush remains devoid of true interior talent. What's worse is the fact that the team's run defense hasn't been much better this year, especially with Sweat and Onyemata dealing with injuries that will keep them both out for the majority of the season.
Had New York focused their efforts on addressing the defensive line with players who could both stop the run and rush the passer, or add players who were better fits for New York's scheme, the unit would not be so poor against the run.
Instead, their overcompensation has only hurt the team in the long run.
New York felt that a big reason why the team struggled in 2025 was due to a lack of leadership. They felt adding players who knew what Glenn wanted out of his team was a need for the 2026 offseason.
Players like Demario Davis, Minkah Fitzpatrick, and Geno Smith were brought in to stabilize both sides of the ball. The belief was they would be able to elevate the roster on their own, and keep the team focused in clutch situations.
So how has that worked out?
The team's leadership hasn't been the problem. New York's problems in the clutch still remain. That's because the organization's coaching staff has made decisions that have negatively impacted the organization. Whether it's not using their timeouts properly, challenging low-leverage plays, or disastrous play-calls, the Jets are clearly being held back by their coaching staff.
No amount of player leadership is going to change that reality.
One thing the Jets have done unequivocally well this offseason was adding offensive talent. From Omar Cooper Jr. to Kenyon Sadiq to the arrival of left guard Dylan Parham, New York's offensive weaponry is among the best the organization has seen in decades.
There's a problem, though.
They have a coach who doesn't know how to get the most out of all their talent, or refuses to adjust to the talent on the roster. The organization's lack of creativity offensively sunk the organization's chances before they took their first snap.
Even as the team found success running the football, it hasn't changed the end result of a bottom-10 offense. The fact that they have been unwilling and unable to shift their offensive focus to what their roster is best suited for shows their lack of imagination.

title: Jets Are Still Saying All the Wrong Things Regarding Garrett Wilson
full_text:
It's not rocket science. Great players need the football as much as possible to put their team in the best position to succeed.
The only team that doesn't seem to understand that is the New York Jets. Gang Green has spent the last several weeks communicating how much they need to get starting receiver Garrett Wilson the football.
The caveat, though, is the team won't sacrifice touches to Wilson if it means the ball has to go to its other playmakers.
"It's only one ball, and Garrett (Wilson) has to get it, Braelon (Allen) has to get it, Sadiq has to get it, Mason (Taylor) has to get it," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said on Friday.
Glenn was speaking mainly about first-round rookie tight end Kenyon Saidq's quiet stretch of games over the last several weeks after a breakout game in Week 3. But his answer, and the one the Jets have given over the last several weeks, show how behind their offensive gameplan really is .
New York spent two of their three first-round picks in the 2026 draft on pass catchers. The group itself is far more talented than it has been in years. Despite the talent, the group has been very inefficient throughout the season, struggling to get the ball to the right matchups, or scheming open their better players.
This is the same offensive staff that confidently boasted they had a plan for their two tight-end sets on offense with Sadiq and Taylor on the field together. They were confident Omar Cooper Jr. could be worked into the offense enough as well.
What we've seen through seven weeks, though, is an offense that simply doesn't know how to scheme their best players open. When offenses are relying on reading defenses to determine who gets the football, they are already one step behind.
In the modern game, offenses should be dictating to the defense what they are going to have to deal with. Not the other way around. It's a fundamental difference why the Jets find themselves 21st in passing. 23rd in yards, and seventh-worst in the league in points scored.
"Throughout my experience, when things go right, I tend to have a part in that," Garrett Wilson said this week. "And when it doesn't, it seems avoidable."
It's not just Wilson who can be targeted and schemed open more. Sadiq, Taylor, and Cooper are all excellent players who can work within an offensive scheme. The problem is the Jets are relying on their quarterback to make reads instead of making it easier for everyone.
Do you think the San Francisco 49ers have trouble getting the ball to their collection of weapons? What about the Los Angeles Rams, or the Green Bay Packers, or every other team with a full collection of star talent?
New York's mindset offensively is one that doesn't work in the modern game. Execution isn't the only way to fix that either. It must be a fundamental shift in how the offense thinks if they are to stress opposing defenses.
The "one ball" excuse doesn't cut it anymore in the NFL.

title: Will McDonald IV's Uncertain Future Has Jets at a Crossroads as Trade Deadline Looms
full_text:
In the NFL, nothing is guaranteed, and for the New York Jets, the future of Will McDonald IV is becoming increasingly uncertain.
The Jets and McDonald are approaching a crossroads, with the organization facing an important decision about whether the pass rusher will remain part of their long-term plans.
The Jets are currently sitting at 2-5. Their playoff hopes are slowly vanishing after a loss to their AFC East rival, the Miami Dolphins. As the season progresses, the team is evaluating its roster and identifying future cornerstones. With the possibility of McDonald being the odd man out.
With the trade deadline approaching, McDonald could be an intriguing trade candidate for general manager Darren Mougey and the Jets if the team decides against pursuing a long-term extension.
The Jets currently hold multiple first-round picks following trades with the Indianapolis Colts and Dallas Cowboys. New York could look to accumulate even more draft capital as the organization continues to assess its future.McDonald could potentially net the Jets more assets in a potential trade.
McDonald, who spent the past three seasons with the Jets, is entering the final year of his rookie contract. The Jets exercised his fifth-year option back in May, keeping him in New York at least through next season.
However, his play on the field could influence whether the Jets view him as a long-term piece of their defense. The remaining games of the season could serve as a litmus test to see if he can be a cornerstone on their defense.
During the 2026 NFL season, he has recorded two sacks and 14 quarterback pressures. That as him  ranked 45th among 133 qualifiers at his position in sacks and 55th in pressures. Much of that production came in the season opener against the Titans.
Since then, he hasn't been as productive as the Jets have hoped in the games following their Week 1 victory.
Throughout his time in New York, McDonald has demonstrated an ability to generate pressure, disrupting the opposing quarterbacks; since entering the league in 2023, he has recorded 23.5 sacks, four forced fumbles, three fumble recoveries, and 84 combined tackles in 54 games played.
That, of course, was under a different coaching staff when Robert Saleh was at the helm in New York.
Gang Green has a tough task facing the Las Vegas Raiders before the Kansas City Chiefs. The Jets also have tough divisional matchups on the schedule as they are set to take on the Buffalo Bills and see the New England Patriots again.
How McDonald performs in these upcoming games could provide further insight into his future with the organization.

title: 3 Key Matchup Will Decide Jets’ Week 8 Outcome vs. Raiders
full_text:
After another disappointing loss last week, the Jets will look to get back into the win column when they take on the Raiders in Week 8.
The last time these two franchises met was in 2023, when Las Vegas defeated New York 16-12. For head coach Aaron Glenn, getting a win against the Raiders is critical . Heading into this matchup with a 5-19 record, a victory against Las Vegas, which enters this matchup on a four-game losing streak, could ease the pressure on his hot seat
There will also be eyes on quarterback Geno Smith, who’s faced criticism over the past few weeks for his play, as he faces his former team.
To turn things around, New York will need to win these three key battles.
The Raiders have one of the league's best passing attacks, ranking fourth in passing yards per game (269), largely thanks to tight end Brock Bowers. Despite missing the first two games, the former Georgia Bulldog leads the team in targets (50), with 34 receptions for 455 yards and three touchdowns.
Since joining Las Vegas in 2024, Bowers has been the team’s best playmaker and go-to pass-catcher. But under first-year head coach Klint Kubiak, he’s utilized Bowers more as a receiver than a tight end, and it’s helped him find greater success.
In his first two seasons, Bowers played 39% and 42.6% of his snaps inline, whereas he’s lined there just 14.9% this season , per Pro Football Focus. Lining him up on the perimeter has given Bowers more one-on-one opportunities, allowing him to exploit linebackers and safeties with slants, posts, and crossing routes.
With more opportunities to move the chains on the outside, Bowers is averaging a career-high 13.4 yards per reception.
The Jets won’t stop Bowers, as Kubiak will find ways to get him involved. But if New York is to have a sliver of a chance, its defense must limit his impact by tightening up the middle.
Per NFL Next Gen Stats , 33.7% of Bowers’s routes have been vertical , ranking second among tight ends with at least 100 routes. Quarterback Kirk Cousins ideally likes to target Bowers on underneath crossers and slants, but he’s also looked to him downfield for explosive plays.
New York’s secondary has struggled against tight ends over the past two weeks, allowing four catches for 48 yards and a touchdown to Patriots TE Hunter Henry and five receptions for 86 yards to Dolphins TE Greg Dulcich.
With the Jets running man coverage at the eighth-highest rate , per Sharp Football Analysis, Glenn must consider mixing in more zone coverage and pressing Bowers at the line of scrimmage. Disrupting his release could throw off his timing and prevent him from getting an opening, while zone coverage would make it harder for Cousins to target him downfield.
Against zone coverage, the Raiders have used Bowers more on short option routes, out routes, and screen plays to get the ball in his hands and let him create yards after the catch. While these adjustments won’t eliminate Bowers from the game, they could make it more difficult for him to generate explosive plays.
If New York allows Bowers to exploit them in one-on-one matchups, don’t be surprised if he has a big game.
Geno Smith has been one of the more efficient quarterbacks this season. Through seven games, the 14-year veteran has completed 70% of his passes for 1,623 yards, 10 touchdowns, and two interceptions.
For the most part, Smith has played well and kept the ball out of harm’s way; however, he’s played too conservatively. Smith hasn’t been nearly as aggressive as he was with the Seahawks, attempting just 17 passes of 20 yards or more, and has often settled for easy checkdowns instead of pushing the ball downfield.
He’s also made occasional poor decisions, such as holding the ball too long in the pocket and taking sacks. We can’t entirely blame Smith for this, as the Jets’ receivers have struggled consistently to create separation.
But if New York is to get back into the win column, then Smith must target Las Vegas’ secondary. The unit was instrumental in the team’s 3-0 start but has remarkably declined over the past four weeks.
During this stretch, the Raiders have allowed 11 passing touchdowns, 252.5 passing yards per game, and a 69% completion rate. According to Next Gen Stats , the Raiders have increased their man coverage rate to 32.1% of passing plays , but have yielded a 54.5% success rate against man.
With Las Vegas struggling to contain opposing passing attacks, Smith must take advantage by pushing the ball downfield and attacking one-on-one matchups, as he’s averaging 9.4 yards per attempt and has thrown six touchdowns against man coverage this season.
That means targeting star receiver Garrett Wilson more, especially as he’s grown increasingly frustrated with his lack of targets over the past two weeks. We saw in Week 3 against the Lions how effective the connection can be against a weak secondary.
Smith connected with Wilson on 10 passes (13 targets) for 107 yards and a touchdown. While protecting the football remains critical, Smith cannot be overly protective.
Week 3 and last week against Miami showed that the Jets are at their best when they stretch the field and attack downfield. Generating enough offense against a struggling Raiders’ secondary will be crucial if New York hopes to come away with a win.
This matchup got increasingly more interesting when Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty said that they can "definitely get the run going" against the Jets .
Well, he’s not wrong. After giving up just 131 rushing yards in the first two games, New York has allowed 763 rushing yards over its last five games and ranks 24th against the run this season, allowing 127.7 rushing yards per game.
In this five-game stretch, the Jets are 1-4, and in all four of their losses, the defense has given up over 100 rushing yards. Until New York improves its play at the line of scrimmage, opposing teams will continue to prioritize the run against them.
For Jeanty, of all people, to express confidence in the team’s ability to run against the Jets speaks volumes about how vulnerable the unit has become.
Since posting 102 rushing yards in the season opener, the former sixth overall pick has struggled to get anything going on the ground. In the last six games, he’s managed just 226 rushing yards, two rushes of 10 yards or more, and an abysmal 2.7 yards per carry.
Jeanty’s not entirely to blame for the Raiders’ struggles on the ground, as the offensive line hasn’t consistently created open running lanes. Another factor is that Kubiak has primarily used  Jeanty to run inside the tackles, while he defers to backup running back Mike Washington Jr. for outside runs.
Given these predictable tendencies, the Jets must prioritize winning at the line of scrimmage and getting to Jeanty early. New York has struggled with missed tackles this season, with linebackers Demario Davis and Jamien Sherwood combining for 17, and must prevent Jeanty from reaching the second level.
Although Jeanty hasn’t reached the second level much this season, he can exploit the Jets with his home-run ability. If the Jets can close the running lanes and make Jeanty indecisive in the backfield, they could force Las Vegas to be one-dimensional and depend on Cousins to move the ball downfield.

title: Growing Will McDonald IV Trade Buzz Leaves Jets With Pros & Cons to Consider
full_text:
We're less than two weeks away from the NFL Trade Deadline. Teams like the Jets must determine if they are willing to be buyers or sell off some of the talent on the roster.
In the case of edge rusher Will McDonald IV (who's without a contract extension and has been involved in trade rumors), Sports Illustrated 's Albert Breer provided an update of sorts . At this time, the Jets are looking to stay where they are with their talent, including their former first-round edge rusher.
"The Jets seem alright with standing pat," Breer wrote on Friday. "They’ve gotten significant interest in fourth-year edge rusher Will McDonald IV but haven’t budged at all."
Things can change quickly, of course.
No one believed the team would trade both Sauce Gardner and Quinnen Williams last year before agreeing to terms with the Cowboys and Colts.
Could a similar situation happen to McDonald if the Jets were to lose games leading up to the deadline?
There are both pros and cons to a potential move.
The NFL is a "what have you done for me lately" kind of league. A player's skill set and production are only as celebrated as long as they continue to be impactful.
In that case, the Jets have watched McDonald struggle in a make-or-break season. The Iowa State pass rusher has recorded just two sacks this season—well below his normal average at the start of his NFL career. His struggles as a run defender, much maligned over the years, have gotten better, but not nearly well enough to warrant a lucrative contract extension.
If anything, it shows that the Jets may be willing to move on from McDonald if the price is right.
Whether head coach Aaron Glenn survives another year or not in his role with the Jets, McDonald doesn't appear to be part of the team's long-term plans. Instead of waiting to figure that out, the team could simply hope to get value from him instead of waiting three years for a compensatory pick when McDonald hits free agency.
It's the only way to get value for a struggling player.
New York is limping into Sunday's contest against the Raiders. David Bailey has a groin injury that has caused him to miss the last three practices. Defensive tackle T'Vondre Sweat is dealing with a knee injury , and Joseph Ossai has been an injured nonfactor for most of his first season in New York.
It's not like the Jets can really afford to give away another edge rusher, especially one who can play on Sunday.
There are other factors in play, though.
McDonald has another year on his contract with a projected $14.4 million cap hit , per Spotrac , which means the asking price will be higher than if he were on an expiring deal. New York's defensive line has also been a major disappointment, needing as many edge rushers as they can.
While McDonald's numbers do not exactly help the Jets' defense, he's still someone who can get after the quarterback.
Any move, therefore, would open a further move that would need to be made during the offseason.
One could argue the Jets were going to need another pass rusher anyway, this offseason, but for a team trying to save its coaching staff's jobs, trading away a player who can make a positive impact does the exact opposite.

title: David Bailey Injury Uncertainty Could Force One Jets EDGE Into Week 8 Spotlight
full_text:
The Jets will likely face the Raiders shorthanded in Week 8 after star rookie pass rusher David Bailey missed Friday's practice and is doubtful for Week 8 , according to The Athletic 's Zack Rosenblatt. The number-two pick has been New York's primary pass-rushing threat . Bailey has 5.5 sacks through seven weeks, leaving the Jets looking for production if he misses time.
In comes third-year man Nate Lynn, who has a chance to make a name for himself after a promising Week 7 performance. The 24-year-old will likely take on a bigger role after Bailey's injury, so the Jets will need him to build on the promise he showed against the Dolphins.
Lynn had himself a party against Miami in Week 7. The undrafted EDGE got his first career sack and graded highest among Jets defenders with a mark of 89.0, according to Pro Football Focus . Lynn made an impact in a smaller role; he will have to show he can step up when the team needs him against Las Vegas.
The Jets will no doubt miss Bailey. The rookie disruptor has accounted for over a quarter of the team's sacks this season, so the pass rush will look less dynamic without the former Red Raider. However, it gives Lynn a chance to prove he can fill the shoes of an end who gets legitimate playing time.
While Lynn performed in the game against Miami, he only played three defensive snaps. He must show that his success wasn't a flash in the pan, but something with substance. With the team struggling in the win-loss column and New York likely missing one of its young stars, Lynn must take on a bigger role if the Jets want to succeed in Week 8 .
The Raiders are not a bad team to see on the other sideline if the Jets are looking for a breakout game from Lynn. The Raiders' offensive line has been ripe for the taking, despite the team's improved 2026 record. With Las Vegas' shaky offensive line and a running back averaging 3.1 yards per carry, Lynn could wreck the game on Sunday.
Las Vegas has struggled to block in the passing game so far this season. While they haven't given up many sacks, the team ranks 28th in pass protection on PFF . The Dolphins rank just behind them, so Lynn and the rest of the Jets' defensive line should have their ears pinned back. Lynn and the Jets could be primed for a breakout game against a team with a struggling offensive line and a far-from-mobile QB.
Sacks are great, but stopping the run wins football games. The Jets struggled in that area against Miami, with Ollie Gordon II going for 100-plus yards and a touchdown. They have a chance to bounce back this week against the Raiders. Despite the big talk , Ashton Jeanty hasn't really excelled for the Silver and Black this season.
If Lynn is to get more time on the field, he must shine against this Raiders' offense. Las Vegas has been shaky establishing the run and protecting the ball in the passing game. Lynn looked good against the Jets' AFC East rival last week, and now he has the chance to improve his outlook in an expanded role against the Raiders.

title: 9 Eagles Observations After Commanders Hand Philly a 6th Straight Loss in Week 8 SNF
full_text:
Move over Andy Reid’s 2012 team. You have company. The Eagles lost their sixth straight game on Sunday night , and that is the first time the organization has lost this many in a row since Reid’s last year, when the losing streak reached eight.
The Eagles went 4-12 and Reid was fired after that dismal season.
The Eagles are now 2-6 after Sunday night’s 27-10 loss to the host Commanders. They went winless in October and started November with another loss. They haven’t tasted victory since Sept. 20, when Jalen Hurts drove the offense for a game-winning touchdown against the Titans in Nashville.
It’s fair to wonder if head coach Nick Sirianni will suffer the same fate as Reid did in 2012. Yes, the Eagles are banged up, but nothing seems to be getting better. Maybe in small snippets they do, but not enough to find a way to win a game.
There are too many mistakes, such as left tackle Jordan Mailata not lining up on the line of scrimmage on a 36-yard field goal made by Jake Elliott. Pushed back five yards, Elliott hit the top of the left upright with about nine minutes to play, keeping the score at 16-10.
The effort seemed better, but again, that didn’t help win a game. The run defense was still not nearly good enough, allowing the Commanders to run for 135 yards, and the offense still cannot find a consistent rhythm.
The Eagles jumped to a 10-0 lead, doing all their scoring in the first quarter, but they couldn’t score a single point over the final three quarters. The Commanders methodically scored 27 unanswered points, getting four field goals from rookie kicker Drew Stevens.
Making his third start, quarterback Tanner McKee was again too inconsistent. He had a costly fumble late in the third quarter just as the Eagles had pulled into a long-range field-goal attempt at minimum. Rookie Markel Bell allowed the strip-sack. McKee, who also threw an interception, was sacked five times.
The Commanders cashed the turnover into a field goal and a 16-10 lead with 1:33 to go in the third quarter.
1. Three-and-outs: The Eagles had fewer of them. After going three-and-out on their first possession, the offense had just one more.
2. Points: The Eagles doubled their first-quarter point output for the season, putting up 10 points. They had been outscored 40-10 coming in and now it’s 43-20 after taking a 10-3 lead into the second quarter.
3. Fumble recovery: The Eagles finally got one. It happened in the first quarter when Drew Mukuba belted tight end Chig Okonkwo after catching the ball. Zack Baun fell on it to set up the offense at the 26, and they turned it into a 3-yard touchdown run by Saquon Barkley.
FUMBLE 🗣️ Zack Baun recovers for the Eagles! PHIvsWAS on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/CbAEhq9j0k
The Eagles were the only team in the NFL not to recover a fumble. That streak is over. Still, it was just the fourth turnover the defense has forced all season.
4. First road start: It was McKee's first start on the road,  and he entered the game for the first time not trailing. He led the offense to 10 points before the Commanders got off the deck and started carving up the Eagles’ defense. McKee cooled off, too, and the Eagles didn’t do anything after that.
5. Eli Stowers: Hey, the rookie tight end made his first catch, which went for seven yards on second-and-six in the third quarter. He finished with three catches for 53 yards.
6. Tyler Steen: The offensive line struggled mightily even though Washington was without the injured Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw, but Steen’s play was particularly glaring. And not in a good way.
7. Unblocked pressure: The Eagles allowed a pivotal sack in the first half when it appeared the offensive line slid right, allowing a free rusher to sack McKee. It was Landon Dickerson who stepped right, allowing the rusher to get home. That could either be a bad scheme by line coach Chris Kuper or a miscommunication about what the Commanders were showing. Maybe both.
8. Pass rush: It’s still too inconsistent, though it showed some life. Jalen Carter notched a big sack to force a punt midway through the third quarter. It was his fourth of the season to take over the team lead, one ahead of Nolan Smith.
Jalen Carter and Jonathan Greenard teaming up for the SACK! PHIvsWAS on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/QB0jrdQCHq
Smith forged back into a tie with a fourth-quarter sack. The outside linebacker also clobbered Jayden Daniels at the end of the first half on a dropback. Still, the Eagles have 10 sacks this season.
Oh, there was a Jonathan Greenard sighting but only because he jumped offsides to negate an interception from Mukuba in the end zone.
9. Third downs: The worst team in the league at converting third downs at 30.9%, the Commanders converted five of 13 (38.5%).

title: Eagles-Commanders Stock Market: Collapse Continues in DC
full_text:
LANDOVER, MD - After a 2-0 start this season, the Eagles are now 2-6 after losing a sixth straight game in the shadow of the nation's capital against the Washington Commanders.
In a microcosm of the season, Philadelphia got off to a 10-0 start on Sunday night and never scored again en route to an ugly 27-10 setback.
A very limited team due to circumstance that has included everything from significant injury attrition to questionable coaching and the retirement Land Johnson, the once powerful Eagles were outgained for the eights consecutive time this season with the Commanders piling up 339 yards to 268 for Philadelphia, the latter number buoyed by the garbage time of the last drive of the night.
The Eagles are now 0-2 in a key three-game stretch against NFL East foes in what's considered a bad division, a run that will finish against the first place New York Giants (4-2-1), who will be coming off their bye week next Sunday.
With tonight's loss, the Eagles are now at the bottom of the division. Dallas (3-5) is in second despite losing to Arizona in troubling fashion Sunday, and the Commanders leapfrogged the Eagles with their second win (2-4-1).
SAQUON BARKLEY'S HEART - There wasn't much to like in this game but Barkley played despite hamstring and back injuries because he felt he could and that his team needed him. In a Super Bowl-or-bust society, the fact that Barkley didn't embrace the tanking mentality is the kind of culture setter that is meaningful in the NFL.
It wasn't great statistically -- 13 carries for 30 yards and a reception for 24 yards -- but the lone touchdown was all Barkley with the 24-yard catch on a wheel route and a three-yard scoring run after a turnover.
LONG-SUFFERING WASHINGTON FANS - For years, the Commanders fans have had to take it as their Eagles peers would invade Northwest Stadium and take over. While Washington is not exactly lighting the league on fire, its faithful enjoyed serenading the Eagles fans out of the stadium in the waning moments. It felt like a cleansing for a long-suffering fanbase although the suffering looks far from done inside the Beltway.
ATTENTION TO DETAIL - Nick Sirianni has claimed that the detail hasn't always been there during the Eagles' skid. That showed up in the fourth quarter when a promising drive that could have stolen the game was quickly derailed by a series of mistakes that "take no talent."
Trailing 16-10, Philadelphia was preparing to go for a fourth-and-four conversion at the Washington 13-yard line with 9:04 left in the game. The Eagles were late in the play clock, as Tanner McKee began imploring for the snap. Feeling the urgency rookie right tackle Markel Bell moved early, forcing the Eagles into a 36-yard field goal attempt that Jake Elliott made drilled.
That worst-case would have made it 16-13 with plenty of time to keep pressing but the kick was wiped out because Jordan Mailata was not on the line of scrimmage. The illegal formation backed the kick up five yards and Elliott banged it off the left upright.
The Eagles got nothing out of the drive. In turn, the Commanders responed with an eight play, 45-yard marching, ending with a 42-yard Drew Stevens field goal -- his fourth of the night -- that made it a two-possession game, 19-10, with only 3:43 remaining.
PLAY ACTION - Everyone should have someone who believes in them like Sean Mannion believes in play action. No matter how ugly George Halas' creation looks in Philadelphia, Mannion is going to throw out 13 personnel with poor blocking tight ends and watch his quarterbacks turn their backs to heat-seeking missiles on the blitz.
THE PASS RUSH - It’s almost amazing that the Eagles have not been able to generate any real consistent pressure with an interior that includes Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis and Moro Ojomo, and an edge group of Jonathan Greenard, Nolan Smith and Jalyx Hunt .
The front has been the key to their success for a very long time and the organization invested heaving in Carter, Davis and Greenard this offseason. The Eagles had just three pressures in the first halft and nine total with two somewhat emoty sacks. The lone bright spot was one strong rush by Smith that seemed to rattle Jayden Daniels for a stretch.
In a Vic Fangio defense, the four-man rush has to be significantly better to generate the expected success.

title: Emerging Eagles' Defensive Concern Needs an Answer to End Losing Streak in Week 8
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — Head coach Nick Sirianni found nothing wrong with the Eagles' effort in Monday night’s loss to the Cowboys . Nothing. Nada. Zip.
He stated it unequivocally, too, during the week: “I did not see an effort issue on Monday night. … There were other things. But effort in no way, shape [or] form was an issue here.”
Two days later, Jordan Davis contradicted his coach.
“It was poor from everybody, and that's just simple and plain about it,” the Eagles defensive tackle said. “It was poor.”
Linebacker Zack Baun pulled no punches when asked if the effort level was up to par. “I do not, no,” he said succinctly.
Sirianni is a player's coach, so hopefully he is just saying publicly that there was no issue with effort, and behind the scenes he is harping on it. It was apparent to those who watched the Cowboys dust the Eagles by 17 points that effort was an issue.
The turnaround has to start on Sunday night when the Eagles visit the Commanders in another primetime game.
Is that even possible at this point?
While key offensive players have been injured at historic levels, the Eagles defense has remained mostly healthy—save for Jonathan Greenard, who can’t seem to shake an ankle injury that has dogged him the last few weeks.
There is talent on the defense. It simply didn’t go away overnight.
“When I first got in the league, they let me know the NFL's not easy to win in,” Jalen Carter said. “It's gonna be hard, day in and day out. And this year's proven that it's hard to win in the NFL and that we just gotta change things now, change things around.”
It should start with effort, and the way to turn that around is through leadership. Who in the Eagles’ locker room has stood up to demand that effort on defense?
There’s no issue on the offensive side, where Jordan Mailata stood in the middle of the Lincoln Financial Field locker room shortly after it opened after a loss to the Panthers, telling reporters he would take their questions right then and there. He was still dressed in full pads and was beginning to unlatch his shoulder pads as he took questions.
Saquon Barkley spoke for more than 15 minutes after the loss to Dallas. Landon Dickerson was on the verge of tears after losing to the Cowboys, saying he played horribly.
Meanwhile, the only players on defense who spoke after losing to Dallas were Cooper DeJean and Jihaad Campbell.
Davis said he thinks players aren’t having fun, that they are approaching things as a “job,” and not enjoying themselves.
“You ask anybody in this locker room, you're not having fun playing the game; it kinda seems like a... That's when it really seems like a job,” Davis said. “When you're having fun, it doesn't seem like a job. It feels like something that you get to do; you have to enjoy this game. It's gonna be wins and losses and everything, and that's in life. You have to find those little moments to enjoy, and right now we're trying to find those little moments, those little wins.”
Nakobe Dean was the player who held everyone accountable. The linebacker made sure his teammates were having fun, whether he was on the sidelines, in practice, in the locker room, or in a game.
This isn’t to relitigate the decision to let Dean walk in free agency to Las Vegas on a three-year, $36 million contract. It's simply to ask: who is the leader of the defense? That is to be determined. Maybe it will be Davis.
“We know what we're capable of,” he said. “We've reached the highest of highs. We've seen the lowest of lows now. We have to do something to fix it, and that's one of the things that we've been a part of in practice this week: fixing the effort. We have to give effort.”

title: Eagles Need Saquon Barkley More Than Ever as Banged-Up RB Room Remains a Week 8 Concern
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — With the Eagles sitting at 2-5 and hamstring and back injuries that cost him two days of practice this week, an average superstar would likely shut things down and live to play another day.
That’s not Saquon Barkley, the pro’s pro who doesn’t even have a game status for Sunday night against the Commanders despite dealing with the kind of nagging issues that will have him on a pitch count.
"One day I'm not gonna be playing football,” Barkley said at his locker on Friday. “Whenever that is, I don't want to look back and be like, 'I could have gave it a chance, and I didn't.'
“That's kind of what I live by. So try my best to just keep recovering, being smart. But I like playing football. So if I have the opportunity to play, I'll try my best to play."
Barkley was able to practice in a limited fashion on Friday after missing the first two days of the week and was removed from the injury report.
The 29-year-old said that he feels “decent” after a week of rehab.
Barkley suffered the hamstring injury early in the Oct. 4 loss to the Rams and missed the next two games. He returned Monday night against the Cowboys on a limited pitch count. Despite that, he performed with remarkable efficiency, rushing seven times for 62 yards and a touchdown, and adding two catches for nine yards before exiting with back tightness.⁠
Barkley said he tweaked the hamstring on his first carry against the Cowboys , a 29-yard run, and later dealt with back issues while trying to compensate.
“Definitely dealing with some stuff, but just working through it,” Barkley said.
He described the recovery as non-linear and said he has stayed focused by “attacking the day, every single day” and remaining “obsessed with my process and my rehab.”⁠
In Landover, Barkley expects to manage the injuries during the game by following the coaches’ plan and keeping his body activated.
“When I was out there, I felt like I was able to provide a spark and make some plays,” he said of his limited action against Dallas.
Through five games this season, Barkley has 244 rushing yards on 43 carries for a 5.7-yard average and one touchdown, plus six receptions for 17 yards. He has been effective when on the field but has had only two or three fourth-quarter carries all season, an area he called a source of frustration.⁠
Barkley understands his value reaches beyond production and into the intangible world of presence.
“That’s one of my best qualities,” he said. “I feel like I have a really good gift of being close with the offense and the defense.”⁠
The Eagles’ running back room has been thinned badly by injuries.
Primary Barkley backups Tank Bigsby (abdomen), Will Shipley (foot) and Dameon Pierce (undisclosed) are on injured reserve. The team also recently reached an injury settlement with Carson Steele and waived him.
Barkley said he has “never seen anything like this” in terms of the attrition at the position and praised the efforts of remaining options expected to help him against the Commanders, veteran practice squad addition Elijah Mitchell and recent 53-man roster promotion Jaydon Blue.
Barkley’s presence could provide a boost for an offense that has ranked near the bottom of the league in several categories as the Eagles try to halt a five-game skid, the worst stretch in the Nick Sirianni era.
“Saquon's an unbelievable player,” quarterback Tanner McKee said. “Obviously, we feel confident with everybody that we have back there. But Saquon's very special, and he makes special plays. He makes a lot of guys miss. He's a vocal leader. He also leads by example and he's an unbelievable player. And so he makes a lot of plays that most people in the NFL can't make.”
