title: 3 Keys to a Surprise Titans Win Over the Bengals in Week 8
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans aren't expected to come out on top in Week 8, to say the least. The NFL's Preview Picks are 10-0 in favor of the Cincinnati Bengals, with not a single prediction even allowing the Titans the benefit of a single-digit loss.
It's an anticipated blowout across the board, but Tennessee can't be counted out just yet. This is a team with their backs against the wall coming off a trade that, from all angles, is meant to improve the roster down the road. Will a cornered group finally fight back this week?
We won't know until tomorrow, but here are three boxes Tennessee would have to check if they were to pull off a surprise victory on Sunday.
Tony Pollard is coming off his best game of the season for Tennessee, and one of the best games of his career. With Tyjae Spears confirmed to sit, Brian Daboll's offense should continue to lean into their veteran RB without a shadow of a doubt.
Will Pollard replicate his career-high-tying, three-touchdown showing in Cincy? Probably not, but he doesn't necessarily need to in order to put Tennessee in a solid position to compete.
So long as Pollard is able to chunk out medium gains and capitalize when he's called on in late-drive, short-yardage situations (assuming the Titans get into those scenarios), he'll have checked his box. Daboll should be scheming heavily for Pollard if Tennessee is to stay afloat on the road.
Of course, forcing a turnover without Jeffery Simmons is going to be a whole lot harder. But last week, the Titans' two takeaways were generated by CB Cor'Dale Flott and LB Anthony Hill Jr.
Both those guys are running it back this week. On the defensive side of the ball, Tennessee has to continue finding ways to disrupt. This is especially crucial in taking on the Bengals' elite offense.
Having scored 30+ points two straight weeks, the Joe-Burrow-led Bengals will attempt to carve the Titans up by way of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins every chance they get. Cincinnati is fifth in passing yards per game in the NFL, with an average of 264.
It's the tallest task to ask of a unit short Simmons. Even so, Robert Saleh was brought to Nashville on the basis of his defensive expertise. If the Titans ever needed a great defensive scheme to cover up holes in the personnel, it's in Week 8.
Cam Ward doesn't have to be electric this week. Again, the Titans will fare the best if they're able to stay in this contest by way of Pollard's work on the ground.
But the Titans still need Ward to be better than he has been. Tennessee needs consistency. The second-year QB has thrown a pick in five straight contests; doing away with his mistakes, as well as working against Tennessee's typically abysmal first halves, would go a long way.
If Ward can come out warm - not necessarily hot - and put enough pressure on the Bengals' defense that opposing DC Al Golden doesn't just stack the box to stop Pollard on every important down, he should at least be able to stop this thing from getting out of hand.
Factor in a flipped field or two from the defense, and you never know... even if you feel like you almost certainly do.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Staff Predictions for Titans vs. Bengals: Faith in a Tennessee Win is Lost After Simmons Trade
full_text:
It's a dour week of staff predictions here at Titans On SI, as we all collectively mourn the team's loss of DT Jeffery Simmons. The Titans are bound to take a hit due to trading away their best player, and that hit comes to a head against the Cincinnati Bengals tomorrow.
Last week, the staff went 1/4 due to Tennessee losing to the Browns. Isaiah was the only one to forecast a Titans loss. This week, the rest of us are following his lead.
With multiple key players confirmed to sit for the Titans and big roster questions still looming, here's our slate of predictions for Tennessee vs. Cincinnati in Week 8.
I'm both highly optimistic about the future of this Titans team and terribly pessimistic about their current state. You don't trade Jeffery Simmons and get away with it now and later. I think Tennessee pays for his loss in Week 8.
The Cincinnati Bengals have scored 30+ points in two straight weeks, and against a freshly weakened Tennessee defense, I expect that trend to continue. Cam Ward is likely to struggle without Carnell Tate, but the Titans' offense should be able to find relative momentum between the red-hot Tony Pollard and reliable second-year WR Elic Ayomanor
I just can't imagine this one going the Titans' way, even then.
Fresh off a competitive loss to the Browns, where the offense scored a season-high 24 points, it's hard not to feel optimistic heading into Cincinnati. However, I believe the Titans are already punting on the season, especially after dealing their best player, DT Jeffery Simmons, to Chicago this week.
The Bengals are top-10 in points scored and fewest points allowed, which is not an ideal matchup for Tennessee. I can't trust QB Cam Ward to keep the Titans in the game. The Bengals are a high-powered offense led by QB Joe Burrow, who boasts a 4-1 record all time against Tennessee.
Following the franchise-altering trade of DT Jeffery Simmons, the Titans have the chance to prove a lot of doubters wrong on Sunday. Unfortunately, this game is a complete mismatch on paper, especially now that Simmons is gone and WR Carnell Tate being ruled out with a shoulder injury.
It’s the type of game that can get out of hand relatively quickly if Tennessee doesn’t come out firing. QB Cam Ward will likely need to match the Bengals’ offensive firepower, and without Tate, an already tall task ultimately becomes too much to overcome.
In the end, I think a strong performance by QB Joe Burrow and company results in a hardly competitive 20-point win at home.
After trading Jeffery Simmons, I expect Tennessee to come out with extra motivation for this game. The Titans should be able to this contest close, but at the end of the day, Cincinnati possesses too much talent and explosiveness on offense.
With how Brian Daboll's offense has played this season, a shoutout with the Bengals isn't winnable for Tennessee.

title: Commanders Report Card: Who Delivered in Eagles Win — and Who Still Fell Short?
full_text:
The first few minutes of the Washington Commanders' attempt at revenge over the rival Philadelphia Eagles seemed to hit every last beat of what Washington fans didn't want to see in the squad's humiliating return to the primetime slate.
They made plenty of mistakes on their first few drives, but look no further than their very first series for a who's-who of classic errors that have regularly peppered Commanders games all season. Jayden Daniels missing on makeable throws, back-to-back false starts, surrendered once-friendly field position on third-and-one, and a blown kick by increasingly inconvenienced kicker Drew Stevens ruled the drive moot, all while backup Eagles quarterback Tanner McKee moved the ball upfield on the defense.
But the second the Commanders, down multiple scores, heard the boos from inside their own house at Northwest Stadium, they erased yet another slow start. Unlike in their previous loss to the San Francisco 49ers, they never took their foot off the gas, scoring 27 straight and somehow climbing right back into the divisional standings at 2-4-1 behind a complicated, well-rounded win.
Daniels looked generally lethargic at first, specifically during one of the false-start calls he initiated with a strange pre-snap pump-fake , but he mostly made the right plays from then on once he exorcised that gaffe from his system. Fans can't quibble with a stat line of 217 yards on 16/29 passing with a touchdown thrown in if he can perform as surgically as he did past the first quarter.
Jayden Daniels ➡️ Stefon Diggs for the TD! PHIvsWAS on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Okl6kfEkFL
That pass to Stefon Diggs was just the tip of the iceberg in Daniels' unflappable passing aggression. He stuck with Treylon Burks for a 53-yard gain after an early drop and kept finding Chig Okonkwo for bailout opportunities, using his receivers' varying strengths to interchange big plays with short-range reads.
This wasn't the cleanest overall outing he's completed in Washington, but Commanders fans have to feel relieved that one of the more subtly frustrating statistics surrounding the team can finally vanish; despite his best (if inconsistent) efforts, he'd yet to secure a win since Week 5 in 2025 , having had to watch backup Marcus Mariota secure this roster's lone previous victory over the Seattle Seahawks on the sidelines while the usual starter recovered from a dislocated elbow. This division win, the first of the Commanders' campaign in four tries, belongs to him as much as anyone.
Even if Jacory Croskey-Merritt were active enough to take his regular spot in the depth chart ahead of spot-starting back Rachaad White, the consensus around the Commanders' less-than-inspiring run game still likely wouldn't be very optimistic given their infrastructure. Whether it's a lack of high-end rushing talent, blockers struggling to create the necessary holes, or both excuses working in tandem, this element of the offense has yet to jump off the screen.
White ended the night with a team-high 55 yards on the ground, but just about all of that chunk yardage and the touchdown it resulted in arrived on Washington’s late, game-clinching drive. Older reserves Austin Ekeler and Jeremy McNichols added 57 more rushing yards, barely enough to punch the spiraling Eagles defense where it hurt.
The new top-three receiving trio post-Terry McLaurin did not disappoint. Following Burks' early flubbed attempt at a simple catch-and-run, a blunder that once looked like an omen for another tough showing out on the field, he, Diggs, and Antonio Williams did well to convert on the chances that Daniels passed their way.
They settled into zones, caught in stride with their passes and held their own against a usually feared Philadelphia secondary. The Eagles, who have often held up against big plays over their contending years, still had 2025 Pro Bowler and All-Pro cornerback Quinyon Mitchell to disrupt the Commanders' wideouts, but even he arguably got the worst of it when Burks burnt him on a deep route.
Quinyon Mitchell is a decent CB at best and Eagles fans will act like he’s playing like 09’ Darrelle Revis pic.twitter.com/V7HlEB7hVP
The receiving room may yet survive and enjoy some thrills without McLaurin, who's slated to miss the remainder of the season following a torn patellar tendon against the 49ers, meaning that Washington will take whatever they can get out of its prospects and supplementary veterans. As it turns out, their scheme heading forward heavily involves Okonkwo, and he's ready for Daniels' heaves.
32 yards on two completions on four targets doesn't look like much, but the tight end always seemed to be available whenever Daniels needed a savior out deep. That's where Okonkwo's size came in handy, with few individual defenders able to deter someone with his agility and hands. Had he not coughed up a tough fumble on one of his receptions, this could have easily gone down as the big receiver's most impactful outing of the 2026 slate.
CHIG OKONKWO ALMOST HAD ONE pic.twitter.com/hp1UGVPaQr
His double-catch to help Washington escape its own end zone already seemed like a special grab in the moment, and that was before he came within a foot of collecting a play-of-the-year contender with a goal-line fade attempt for the ages. The tight end rotation has desperately needed anyone to aid Daniels' pass-catching corps, and Okonkwo finally seems at home in Washington's offense.
At the very least, Washington's offensive linemen allowed the quarterback to sit back and watch routes develop a few times, a luxury that fans have come to appreciate given his slight frame and their lack of reliable blocking.
Even if Philadelphia's pass-rushers still made life tough for the tackles, this grade is a procedural, pre-snap-related indictment of the position group's composure. This unit is far too handsy in drawing holding calls and much too jumpy with Daniels calling the shots, with the false starts repeatedly hurting the offense's chances of converting on their promising drives.
Still, only two sacks in Daniels' game recap have to be mentioned when discussing a blocking line that's not completely untalented- just undisciplined.
Everyone enjoyed moments to shine against an Eagles offense that seemed to disintegrate as the game trudged on. McKee went down five times to sacks from Commanders tacklers, largely because Washington emphasized rushing the quarterback's distribution process.
There were the usual suspects, like regular edge presences like Odafe Oweh and K'Lavon Chaisson, but then there were breakouts like Charles Omenihu in his best Commanders appearance yet and Shy Tuttle, the impressive veteran who continues shining since barely sneaking onto the roster . The strength in numbers, particularly from versatile middle linebackers Sonny Styles and Frankie Luvu, empowered plenty of niche defenders to get in on the action within the deceptive scheme and keep the Eagles' own stoppers guessing.
This unit didn't have as much to do as in Week 1, when Eagles receiver DeVonta Smith was active in Philadelphia, but they still made their collective presence known within the blitzing attack. Nick Cross was everywhere as the much-appreciated safety who can split defenders at scrimmage, as was Amik Robertson in his typically loud breakups on screen pass attempts.
Trey Amos , now that his return game against San Francisco is finally in the past, looked comfortable breaking up his rare targets in isolation, and fans will remember the pick he collected off of Dallas Goedert's hands that was wiped out following a roughing-the-passer penalty. No matter: Rasul Douglas stepped up a few minutes later with an interception that triggered no flags, thereby setting up the final, game-clinching scoring drive in the matchup's closing minutes.
Rasul Douglas with the INT for the Commanders! PHIvsWAS on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/UYdodH2LDO
The one blooper that went down on the special…

title: Commanders Instant Reaction: Depleted Front Delivers the Biggest Answer Against Eagles | Game Pulse
full_text:
After falling behind 10-0, the Washington Commanders scored 27 unanswered points to beat the Philadelphia Eagles 27-10 Sunday night to improve to 2-4-1. The penalties didn’t disappear after the bye , but Washington’s pass rush took over, and Rachaad White finished the job on the ground. With McLaurin out and three defensive tackles unavailable , Washington needed contributions from the players taking on more work. Antonio Williams got involved early , Charles Omenihu made his return count, and Stevens answered his opening miss with four straight makes. Those contributions helped the Commanders overcome another night of costly mistakes and keep their season alive. Here are my immediate reactions in this week’s Game Pulse. *Game Pulse collects my instant takeaways after each quarter and at the final whistle.
The Eagles walk off the field, losers of 6 straight pic.twitter.com/0tT0qYOZAC
- Washington’s defensive front finished this game. Dorance Armstrong was still making plays against the run, and Odafe Oweh beat Jordan Mailata off the edge for a late sack. A season-high five sacks is the production Washington has needed from this group; Washington did it without Daron Payne, Javon Kinlaw, and Jer’Zhan Newton, while holding Saquon Barkley to 30 yards on 13 carries. - Antonio Williams’ 30-yard catch was excellent work finishing the play and keeping the ball off the ground. Washington needed somebody to make that catch, and the rookie delivered. Between his involvement on the touchdown drive and that fourth-quarter gain, Williams gave Jayden Daniels important completions at different stages of the game. - Drew Stevens followed his opening miss with four straight makes, including the 42-yarder that gave Washington a two-score lead. Philadelphia went the other direction, backing itself up with penalties before Jake Elliott hit the upright. Washington benefited from that miss, then made the next possession count. - K'Lavon Chaisson’s late sack helped put Philadelphia in a desperate situation, and Rasul Douglas took advantage when McKee floated a ball up for grabs. Chaisson’s penalties were costly, but he also helped Washington close this game. After having an earlier interception erased by a flag, the defense made this takeaway count. - Rachaad White put it away. His 33-yard run set up the one-yard touchdown, and Washington finished with 27 unanswered points after falling behind 10-0. The penalties still need fixing, but the Commanders turned their last takeaway into a touchdown and finished the job on the ground.
SUUUUUUUUUL pic.twitter.com/oKB3eTFhwW
- Nick Cross and the left side of the defense blew up a run in the backfield, and Sonny Styles later helped hurry McKee into releasing the ball before Omenihu could get there again. Washington is making Philadelphia work for its yards despite the missing pieces up front. - Charles Omenihu made his return count, beating two blockers for his first sack with Washington. Dorance Armstrong then forced a fumble that Omenihu recovered. Those are the kinds of disruptive plays Washington needed from its veteran defensive ends, and both delivered in the third quarter. - Chig Okonkwo practically caught that 22-yarder with three fingers. After his first-quarter fumble, that was a good response and another reminder of what he can give this passing game when Washington gets him involved. - The offensive line still found ways to make things harder. Another presnap flag, followed by Chris Paul getting beaten for a sack, brought back the same problems Washington spent the bye trying to fix. The offense has shown improvement tonight, but those mistakes keep limiting what it can do. - Daniels’ 54-yard connection with Treylon Burks gave Washington a much-needed explosive play, and Stevens finished the possession with a 25-yard field goal. Washington had scored 16 unanswered points. You’d like a touchdown after a gain like that, but the Commanders were finally making Philadelphia chase them. - Chaisson’s second personal foul was especially costly because it wiped out an interception at the end of the quarter. Washington had a chance to take the ball away again and instead gave Philadelphia another opportunity. The defense was doing enough to get off the field; that penalty kept it out there.
Tough break for the Commanders as they get flagged for roughing the passer. You hate to see a player going up to swat a pass and coming down and getting flagged but that's the Roger Goodell experience pic.twitter.com/SODurabvPq
- Antonio Williams caught three passes on the touchdown drive, and Austin Ekeler added an 18-yard run around the outside. That’s a better look at how Washington can keep this offense moving without McLaurin. Williams gave Daniels somewhere to go with the ball, and Ekeler showed why getting him more involved made sense. - The touchdown to Stefon Diggs was a well-designed use of traffic to create separation without drawing an offensive pass interference flag. That’s the pick/not-pick play you want down there. Blough helped free his receiver, Daniels delivered, and Washington finished the opportunity. - Even after scoring, Washington couldn’t get through the extra point without another pre-snap penalty. Then K’Lavon Chaisson created pressure and forced a hurried throw, only to get called for a personal foul afterward. The offense showed some life in the second quarter, but the discipline problems keep following this team. - Luke McCaffrey has helped Washington in the return game. Between his 44-yard kickoff return and 27-yard punt return, he’s giving the offense opportunities to work with a shorter field. - Diggs cutting back inside on his late 20-yard catch was smart with timeouts available. Take the extra yards when Washington still has a way to stop the clock. Daniels took a hard hit along the way, but the Commanders got into position for Stevens’ 38-yard field goal and came away with points before halftime. Daniels looked like he was in some pain after the hit, but he stayed in the game.
Washington is bringing the pressure with an 88% blitz rate. 👀 #NextGenStats powered by @awscloud . pic.twitter.com/rJz9xlHooa
- Two weeks to clean things up, and Washington still turned third-and-1 into third-and-11 with back-to-back false starts. Luke McCaffrey’s 44-yard opening return had set the offense up at midfield, but that opportunity ended with a missed field goal. The later ineligible receiver penalty and Chris Paul’s false start added to a quarter full of avoidable mistakes. - The defense gave Washington something to work with on Philadelphia’s opening possession, getting Tanner McKee off his spot and forcing a three-and-out. With the defensive front missing so many pieces, that was an encouraging start. The offense needed to do more with the opportunities it was getting. - Treylon Burks’ drop hurt, but Daniels had his own miss on the third-down throw to Stefon Diggs. Washington needs both its quarterback and receivers to finish those plays, especially with Terry McLaurin out. There were chances to keep possessions moving. - Chig Okonkwo’s fumble added another mistake from a player Washington needs to lean on. He has become an important part of this passing game, which makes ball security even more important when the offense is already struggling to sustain drives. - Drew Stevens answered his miss from 55 yards by hitting from 56. Good response from the rookie, but Washington keeps asking him to salvage possessions from a long way out. The offense has to give itself a chance to finish closer to the end zone.

I’ll be watching whether the offense gets lined up cleanly and whether first and second down leave it with manageable third downs. Those are changes that should show up before Washington is chasing the game. - With three defensive tackles unavailable and Saquon Barkley cleared to play , this starts up front. Washington’s…

title: 10 Commanders Quotes Reveal What Washington Changed Before Eagles Rematch
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have had nearly two weeks to examine what went wrong during their 1-4-1 start . Now they'll find out whether that extra preparation makes a difference when the Philadelphia Eagles visit Northwest Stadium on Sunday night. From Jayden Daniels identifying problems with the offense's operation to Dan Quinn explaining why both sides of the ball needed simplifying, this week's press conferences offered a clearer picture of what Washington has been working on. Here are 10 quotes that help define where the Commanders stand entering Week 8.
Question: How does Daniels maintain a positive outlook despite the team's difficult start and continued losses? “I mean, to our benefit, you know, we still have an opportunity to, you know, shift our season and, you know, try to win the division. And, you know, you've got to not worry when you look at that, but you've got to take it day by day and, you know, kind of have that optimistic mindset ... Once one gets rolling, hopefully, you know, a lot more follow. So you've just got to take the process day by day and not really try to focus on the outcome. We know what's out there. Like, you know, we're not blind to that, but this is day by day, and as soon as you start thinking about that and you get out of your process, your routine, that's where you kind of get all messed up.”
Question: What will Steve Wilks' role be during Sunday's game, and how will he help the coaching staff? “Just another set of eyes. It won't be something too significant, because he won't be at every game. So he'll be on the sideline. He'll give some information back as we get through the calls, going through the iPad. So it's, you know, just another set of seasoned eyes that we'll have.”
Question: What's been responsible for the improved production from the tight end position, particularly with Chig Okonkwo back? “You know, he's playing at a high level right now. First and second down, he's been, you know, really rolling. We're trying to get him in space, and he certainly, you know, has made the most of his opportunities. So things that we saw on tape as we got him in free agency and then really even into OTAs, we're trying to highlight for him and, you know, certainly want to get him involved more all 60 minutes in the plan.”
Context: Jayden Daniels discusses Terry McLaurin's season-ending injury and its impact on the locker room. “Well, I'll answer your second question first. On the field, it's just next-man-up mentality. It's an unfortunate circumstance, the situation that we're in. You never want to deal with injuries. And I know how hard Terry worked, you know, to get back from what he was dealing with last year and, you know, to have countless conversations with him. And obviously it sucks, and that's just, you know, just what he has to deal with right now, adversity. But I just think to the locker room, to everybody, it's a blow because just Terry, just his energy, his presence, his leadership, just what he means to this organization. Like, you know, having him deal with that, it's going to sting for a little bit, but, you know, we got to hold it down while he's gone.”
Question: What progress has Antonio Williams made over the last several weeks, and how can Washington get him more involved? “Over the few weeks, playing multiple positions, that's a challenge, you know, for any player, especially a first-year player. So to settle in more at one spot, John, that will help also. Get more playing time, more ops, you know, just based on that alone. He's diligent. He's got good feel, how to play it in zone, if the routes have to adjust for man-to-man. Those are, like, some of the subtle things that I see from him.”
Who will help replace the void left by Terry McLaurin in this Commanders offense? May I present to you: Antonio Williams. pic.twitter.com/k0xkFsjAJb
Question: How does Ekeler view the changes Washington made to simplify its offense? “Well, it depends. I feel like it depends on where you're at mentally. If you're a rookie, I think this is still a complex offense. We still have enough variety to have a great game plan. Maybe it's not as many different types of personnel groupings, maybe not as many combinations of different types of players. Maybe make it a little more universal, where multiple people can play at the same spot. And so I think it's something that helps us play faster, but I think it's still an offense that you can go attack and have a diversified game plan. So simplifying it, maybe you're just bringing down 20% of the play calls and play groupings.”
Question: Washington has one of the NFL's highest blitz rates . Why hasn't that resulted in more consistent pass-rush success? “I think there's a combination of a few things. There's the execution of it in terms of the assignments, the paths. There's some winning. We have to win one-on-ones when we get those one-on-one matchups. And so very seldom are you going to have free runners all the time. And so you're going to have to win some one-on-ones. But we can be more useful with that if we're executing properly and attacking the right path, right edges on certain guys.”
Question: How have Daniels' responsibilities changed in the new offense, particularly with checks at the line of scrimmage? “I'd say just having the urgency from myself and obviously everybody else, the subbing and stuff like that, the urgency in and out the huddle is kind of the biggest thing for me where I could grow even more. It's just getting up to the line of scrimmage and, you know, giving us more time, you know, to go out there and dissect and have an idea what the defense is presenting or what they're doing. And I think that's kind of just the biggest thing, like the communication in and out the huddle.”
Question: What were the most important findings from Washington's bye-week offensive evaluation, and what changes can the coaching staff make? “I think without giving too much away, there's some things we can do in personnel groupings to help just allow the players who are on the field to play a little bit faster. So communication improves, simplifying some things there. And then the biggest hangup for us as a unit so far has been third and fourth down. So we've got to be able to, you know, when everybody knows we're going to throw it, we've got to be able to hit our landmarks, protect, throw, catch, coach, play better, you know, coach and execute better at that point.”
Question: When Washington talks about simplifying its schemes, does that mean simplifying the terminology or reducing the responsibilities players have during a play? “Yep, both. I'll give you the first one. Like, sometimes it could be layers. So it could have a call on offense or defense that has, if they do this, we'll do this. If they do this, we'll do this. Sometimes we need something that's like, this is how we're going to go play. And so that would be a volume thing. Say, how many of those do we want checks? That is a part of what we do and why I like our system. But there'll be times where I just want the guys to go play as fast and as decisively as we can. And the same thing on the offensive side. If you're always chasing a certain look, you could lose some aggressiveness or execution. So that's the balance. And so some of it is volume. Some of it is, let's say, layers down to get the execution like you want.”
Washington spent the bye week identifying problems that have followed it through the first six games. The coaching staff has now explained what it intends to do differently, from reducing some of the responsibilities within its schemes to getting calls communicated faster. Sunday night against Philadelphia will provide the first real look at whether any of those changes make a difference. title: Commanders Face a Different Eagles Team — and a Loss Could Cost More Than a Game
full_text:
Two months ago, the Washington Commanders entered Philadelphia with plenty to prove, certainly more so than their first matchup opponents, the formidable Eagles .
Unlike their respectable eastern neighbors, who'd made five consecutive playoff appearances and two Super Bowl runs, including an eventual victory two seasons prior, the Commanders seemed to be teetering on the verge of irrelevancy. Their own surge into momentary greatness was snuffed out by the Eagles on their own road to glory during the 2024 NFC Championship Game, and the following campaign's forgettable 5-12 record signaled that change would be required for D.C. to host a revived winner.
For a few quarters, it seemed like the stepping stones for a classic come-from-behind Jayden Daniels-fueled Commanders win were falling into place. The quarterback overcame a slow start before firing off enough scoring drives to cut the deficit to one score, but an ill-advised play call near the final clock's expiration cost the upstarts any shot at pulling even.
It came down to the wire the last time the Eagles and Commanders met. 👀 📺 Eagles at Commanders: Sunday 7 p.m. ET on NBC & Peacock pic.twitter.com/vqx7IyFa1H
That dramatic finish provided both sides with the results they'd grown accustomed to; while the Commanders received an early loss, the Eagles were handed a season-opening win. And now, with Washington emerging from another break after their Week 7 bye, the 1-4-1 operation plans to seek revenge against its spiraling 2-5 counterpart in an attempt to save its still-breathing season.
The Commanders' recent weeks of faceplants have given plenty to talk about as they try to bag their first victory in over a month, but it's worth diving into which iteration of the Eagles they should expect.
Even though they weren't exactly the Greatest Show on Turf over their last few seasons, their scoring attack has plunged to 15.8 points per game over their five outings, all of which Philadelphia lost. Jalen Hurts' calf injury and subsequent blood clot discovery in Week 5 did no one any favors, as he's unlikely to play again this season while undergoing treatment, leaving backup quarterback Tanner McKee to perform without suddenly-retired, Canton-bound offensive tackle Lane Johnson.
While Saquon Barkley's availability has been spotty over the last month, he's expected to play in the Eagles' rematch against the Commanders. After returning to action against the Dallas Cowboys on Monday Night Football, he and his re-aggravated hamstring were up and practicing again heading into this weekend.
Saquon Barkley (hamstring/back) is practicing today. pic.twitter.com/hpmNVaLQpW
The Commanders' quietly effective run defense still couldn't have been too pleased to see those pictures of the star back's limited run at practice, with Barkley keeping Washington on its toes back in Week 1. He rushed for 83 yards on 15 touches with his typical slipperiness, though no one involved could have known that that would ring in as the former All-Pro's season-high to this point.
We now know the Commanders can hold their own on the ground with their versatile middle linebackers and blitzing options in the secondary, and this week looks like a great opportunity to prove they know exactly who they are.
Aside from not having split their annual season series with the Eagles yet, anyone betting on the Commanders assumes they spent their week off taking a long, hard look at the opportunity presented by the underperforming division ahead of them.
Despite only clinching a win once, a Week 3 upset over the Seattle Seahawks , the Commanders still have fewer losses than the Eagles, thanks to the embarrassing tie hanging on to the end of their numerical record. And unlike the strung-together New York Giants and the second-place Dallas Cowboys, Washington still has some semblance of a defense and their franchise quarterback at its helm.
Though Daniels has heard more than a few complaints about his occasionally inexplicable decision-making, it's hard to argue with the raw numbers he's posted in his two performances after his elbow dislocation. Over 600 all-purpose yards with a completion rate above 70% have resulted in four touchdowns while surviving a patchwork offensive line and continued losses from his pass-catching corps, but the gaffes have buried his generally clutch contributions.
He's much less of a question mark than head coach Dan Quinn , who may be playing for his job by this point in the season. A few of those losses can be pinned on questionable game management, and a fifth defeat in seven games against a hurting Eagles team would likely offer little further job security for the third-year coach. A loss Sunday would drop Washington to 1-5-1, hand Philadelphia a sweep of the season series, and leave the Commanders with just one victory through seven games. With the November 10 trade deadline approaching, Adam Peters would also face a growing question about whether this roster deserves additional help or whether Washington should begin prioritizing the future. That's a difficult position for a team that entered the season expecting to compete for the division.
That decision isn't inevitable yet. Yes, they're still short their starting left tackle in Laremy Tunsil , with few impressive alternatives to boast, and the cornerback rotation is still far from offering anything resembling comfort for the fan base. But the NFC East remains within reach, giving the Commanders a chance to keep their season alive rather than begin looking toward the future. That starts with Quinn's team finally putting some positive consistency together Sunday night.

title: Commanders News: Daron Payne Out as Washington Faces Barkley Without Its Starting DTs | Burgundy Roundup
full_text:
The Commanders went from one starting defensive tackle out against Philadelphia to two in a matter of hours Friday. Javon Kinlaw had already been ruled out with a knee injury when Daron Payne appeared on the injury report with a foot issue. Washington initially listed Payne as questionable, then ruled him out Friday night . Tashan Reed of The Washington Post reported that Payne is expected to miss extended time, with further testing scheduled for Saturday. Jer’Zhan Newton could give Washington another option inside, but his return isn’t automatic. He was limited in practice all week and is questionable as he works back from a torn pectoral. Newton is still on injured reserve , so the Commanders must activate him before he can play Sunday night. Charles Omenihu was limited Friday with groin and ankle injuries but carries no game designation. The Eagles got better news at running back. Saquon Barkley missed practice Wednesday and Thursday with hamstring and back issues, returned Friday on a limited basis , and has no game designation. Philadelphia ruled out five players, including receivers DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks, but Barkley is set to play against a Washington front missing Payne and Kinlaw. How much work he can handle remains a question after those injuries limited him Monday against Dallas. Washington also has a decision to make at receiver. Treylon Burks returned to practice on a limited basis on Friday after missing Thursday, leaving him questionable with a foot injury for the first game without Terry McLaurin. Stefon Diggs practiced fully for the second straight day, while Antonio Williams is expected to take on more work and Van Jefferson has joined the active roster. Burks’s status will help determine how David Blough divides the snaps behind Diggs.
The Washington Commanders are trying to dig out of an early-season hole. Their star quarterback is also trying to break free from a streak nobody ever wants to be a part of, as he hasn't won a game as a starter since October 5, 2025 , against the Chargers, which will be 392 days on Sunday. In that amount of time, Washington is 0-7-1 in his starts, including four injury-interrupted appearances. The team has also had two offensive coordinators during that timeline, with Kliff Kingsbury leaving this past offseason and David Blough being promoted.
As Adam Peters said on 106.7 this morning, Terry McLaurin is undergoing surgery for his torn patellar tendon today. Surgery is in New York. "He's a big part of what we're doing and what we've done," Peters said.
Javon Kinlaw missed practice all week, so it wasn't much of a surprise when the Washington Commanders officially listed him as out on their final injury report Friday. The surprise was Daron Payne, who was added with a foot injury; he was initially listed as questionable after being limited in Friday's practice, then downgraded to out. John Bates, Treylon Burks, and Jer’Zhan Newton were all also listed as questionable for Sunday night's game against Philadelphia.
Adam Peters chatting with Cris Collinsworth (Mike Tirico in the blue shirt, Melissa Stark in the foreground) pic.twitter.com/eUIR2q8L2U
With Terry McLaurin out for the season , a lingering question of who gets his targets now remains unanswered. According to Quinn's comments on Monday: "Antonio [Williams] is one that you'd see getting more targets to go." That's probably true, but with Stefon Diggs and Treylon Burks in the mix, and Van Jefferson just signed to the active roster, the receiving room still looks pretty crowded.
Jayden Daniels is the 8th player in NFL history to have 5+ pass TD, 2+ rush TD and 0 INT in his first four games of a season. He is the only one of those players to not have a winning record in that span, let alone 0 wins pic.twitter.com/JAUgX1zwg2
John is joined by ESPN's Tim McManus, previewing Sunday's Commanders vs. Eagles game. He also talked injury updates, Steve Wilkes role, and more!
Kevin opened the show with why Adam Peters will sweat out Sunday night's game more than anyone else in the organization. Jay Gruden jumped on to talk about the addition of Steve Wilks to the sideline. He previewed and picked the Commanders-Eagles game in addition to giving out his "NFL Lock of the Week".
Lake Lewis Jr. recaps the Washington Commanders Friday practice in preparation for Sunday night's NFC East clash against the Philadelphia Eagles. Lake also gives the teams latest injury report and a late development to a major injury for the team.

title: Commanders' Final Injury Report Takes a Serious Turn Ahead of Eagles Game
full_text:
Javon Kinlaw missed practice all week, so it wasn't much of a surprise when the Washington Commanders officially listed him as out on their final injury report Friday. The surprise was Daron Payne , who was added with a foot injury; he was initially listed as questionable after being limited in Friday's practice. John Bates, Treylon Burks, and Jer’Zhan Newton were all also listed as questionable for Sunday night's game against Philadelphia. UPDATE: Friday evening brought worse news. Tashan Reed of The Washington Post reported that Payne suffered a significant foot injury during practice, will miss Sunday's game, and is expected to miss significant time. NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo also reported that Payne could be headed to injured reserve, with further testing expected Saturday. The team downgraded Payne to out Friday night.
They've now lost Payne and Laremy Tunsil to fluke practice injuries. Tough. https://t.co/WM1IncvgiZ
Newton is still in his 21-day practice window as he returns from a pectoral injury ; the Commanders must still activate him before he's eligible. Bates improved from not practicing at all to limited, while Burks went from limited to not practicing , then back to limited on Friday . Commanders head coach Dan Quinn didn't hide how impressed he was with Newton's recovery work Wednesday: "Man, he has worked his ass off." Luke McCaffrey, Charles Omenihu , and Deatrich Wise Jr. were limited Friday but carried no game designation; Omenihu was limited all week with groin/ankle injuries. Nick Allegretti rebounded from missing Thursday's practice by returning as a full participant Friday. Jayden Daniels, Stefon Diggs, and Marcus Mariota all finished the week as full participants and carry no game designation. Philadelphia has its own injury problems , ruling out five players for Sunday night's game, including receiver DeVonta Smith (hamstring), Jihaad Campbell (hamstring/quad), Britain Covey (knee), Jonathan Jones (hamstring), and Dontayvion Wicks (ankle). Cornerback Jakorian Bennett is questionable with a knee injury, while Saquon Barkley was limited Friday with hamstring/back issues but carries no game designation. Jalyx Hunt (knee/ankle) and Moro Ojomo (neck) were also limited but have no game designation.
